question: What was the federal funds target range after each FOMC meeting in 2025, and at which meetings did the Committee change it?
answer:
The Federal Reserve held the federal funds target range steady at 4-1/4 to 4-1/2 percent for the first five FOMC meetings of 2025, then cut it by 1/4 percentage point at each of the final three meetings, ending the year at 3-1/2 to 3-3/4 percent. The Committee changed the target range at the September 17, October 29, and December 10, 2025 meetings.

| Meeting date | Target range after meeting | Action |
|---|---|---|
| January 29, 2025 | 4-1/4 to 4-1/2 percent | Held steady [D16] |
| March 19, 2025 | 4-1/4 to 4-1/2 percent | Held steady [D23] |
| May 7, 2025 | 4-1/4 to 4-1/2 percent | Held steady [D17] |
| June 18, 2025 | 4-1/4 to 4-1/2 percent | Held steady [D18] |
| July 30, 2025 | 4-1/4 to 4-1/2 percent | Held steady [D19] |
| September 17, 2025 | 4 to 4-1/4 percent | Changed (cut 1/4 point) [D20] |
| October 29, 2025 | 3-3/4 to 4 percent | Changed (cut 1/4 point) [D21] |
| December 10, 2025 | 3-1/2 to 3-3/4 percent | Changed (cut 1/4 point) [D22] |

Details on the changes:
- At the September 17, 2025 meeting, the Committee "decided to lower the target range for the federal funds rate by 1/4 percentage point to 4 to 4-1/4 percent," citing a shift in the balance of risks with downside risks to employment having risen [D20].
- At the October 29, 2025 meeting, it "decided to lower the target range for the federal funds rate by 1/4 percentage point to 3-3/4 to 4 percent," again citing the shift in the balance of risks [D21].
- At the December 10, 2025 meeting, it "decided to lower the target range for the federal funds rate by 1/4 percentage point to 3-1/2 to 3-3/4 percent," for the same stated reason [D22].

The five earlier meetings each used the language "maintain the target range for the federal funds rate at 4-1/4 to 4-1/2 percent" [D16][D23][D17][D18][D19].

Note on voting context (not required for the range itself): the July 30 hold was opposed by Governors Bowman and Waller, who preferred a 1/4-point cut [D19]; the September 17 cut was opposed by Miran, who preferred a 1/2-point cut [D20]; the October 29 cut was opposed by Miran (1/2-point cut) and Schmid (no change) [D21]; and the December 10 cut was opposed by Miran (1/2-point cut) and by Goolsbee and Schmid (no change) [D22].

The evidence covers all eight 2025 FOMC meetings, so no meetings are left unaccounted for.

question: Who dissented at each FOMC meeting in 2025, and what did each dissenter prefer?
answer:
Of the eight regular FOMC meetings in 2025, five had at least one dissent: March 18-19, July 29-30, September 16-17, October 28-29, and December 9-10. The January 28-29, May 6-7, and June 17-18 meetings were unanimous. Notably, the only dissent in the first half of the year (March) was not about the federal funds rate at all, while all dissents in the second half concerned the size of the rate move.

| Meeting (2025) | Committee decision | Dissenter(s) | What each dissenter preferred |
|---|---|---|---|
| Jan 28-29 | Hold at 4-1/4 to 4-1/2% | None (unanimous) | — |
| Mar 18-19 | Hold at 4-1/4 to 4-1/2% | Christopher J. Waller | Same rate (no change to 4-1/4 to 4-1/2%); objected only to the balance-sheet decision, preferring to continue the current pace of securities-holdings reduction rather than slow it |
| May 6-7 | Hold at 4-1/4 to 4-1/2% | None (unanimous) | — |
| Jun 17-18 | Hold at 4-1/4 to 4-1/2% | None (unanimous) | — |
| Jul 29-30 | Hold at 4-1/4 to 4-1/2% | Michelle W. Bowman; Christopher J. Waller | Each preferred a 1/4-point cut to 4 to 4-1/4% |
| Sep 16-17 | Cut 1/4 point to 4 to 4-1/4% | Stephen I. Miran | Preferred a 1/2-point cut to 3-1/2 to 3-3/4% |
| Oct 28-29 | Cut 1/4 point to 3-3/4 to 4% | Stephen I. Miran; Jeffrey R. Schmid | Miran: 1/2-point cut to 3-1/2 to 3-3/4%; Schmid: no change (3-3/4 to 4%) |
| Dec 9-10 | Cut 1/4 point to 3-1/2 to 3-3/4% | Stephen I. Miran; Austan D. Goolsbee; Jeffrey R. Schmid | Miran: 1/2-point cut to 3 to 3-1/4%; Goolsbee and Schmid: no change (3-1/2 to 3-3/4%) |

Supporting detail by meeting:

- January 28-29: The Committee maintained the target range at 4-1/4 to 4-1/2 percent, and the minutes record "Voting against this action: None." [D1][D9]
- March 18-19: The Committee maintained the range at 4-1/4 to 4-1/2 percent. The statement records that "Voting against this action was Christopher J. Waller, who supported no change for the federal funds target range but preferred to continue the current pace of decline in securities holdings." [D3] The minutes add that Waller's view rested on reserve balances being over $3 trillion and no evidence the banking system was near an ample level of reserves; he favored relying on existing tools and a plan for short-run strains rather than changing the QT pace. [D40]
- May 6-7: The Committee maintained the range at 4-1/4 to 4-1/2 percent; the minutes record "Voting against this action: None" (Neel Kashkari voted as an alternate member). [D5][D15]
- June 17-18: The Committee maintained the range at 4-1/4 to 4-1/2 percent; the minutes record "Voting against this action: None." [D18]
- July 29-30: The Committee maintained the range at 4-1/4 to 4-1/2 percent. The statement records that "Voting against this action were Michelle W. Bowman and Christopher J. Waller, who preferred to lower the target range for the federal funds rate by 1/4 percentage point at this meeting" (i.e., to 4 to 4-1/4 percent); Adriana D. Kugler was absent and not voting. [D32] The minutes corroborate the two dissenters and their 25-basis-point preference. [D20][D21]
- September 16-17: The Committee cut 1/4 point to 4 to 4-1/4 percent. The statement records that "Voting against this action was Stephen I. Miran, who preferred to lower the target range for the federal funds rate by 1/2 percentage point at this meeting" (i.e., to 3-1/2 to 3-3/4 percent). [D35][D42] The minutes confirm one member voted against, preferring a 1/2-point cut. [D23]
- October 28-29: The Committee cut 1/4 point to 3-3/4 to 4 percent. The statement records that "Voting against this action were Stephen I. Miran, who preferred to lower the target range ... by 1/2 percentage point at this meeting, and Jeffrey R. Schmid, who preferred no change to the target range" (Miran to 3-1/2 to 3-3/4 percent; Schmid to hold at 3-3/4 to 4 percent). [D37][D43] The minutes confirm two dissenters, one favoring a 1/2-point cut and the other no change. [D26]
- December 9-10: The Committee cut 1/4 point to 3-1/2 to 3-3/4 percent. The statement records that "Voting against this action were Stephen I. Miran, who preferred to lower the target range ... by 1/2 percentage point at this meeting; and Austan D. Goolsbee and Jeffrey R. Schmid, who preferred no change to the target range" (Miran to 3 to 3-1/4 percent; Goolsbee and Schmid to hold at 3-1/2 to 3-3/4 percent). [D39][D44] The minutes confirm three dissenters: two preferring no change and one preferring a 1/2-point cut. [D29][D30]

Note on the derived ranges: the statements specify the size of each dissenter's preferred cut (1/4 or 1/2 point) or "no change" rather than always stating the resulting range; the specific target ranges shown for the 1/2-point-cut dissenters (3-1/2 to 3-3/4 percent in September and October; 3 to 3-1/4 percent in December) follow directly from applying the stated cut to the then-current range.

question: How did the Beige Book's overall assessment of economic activity change across the eight editions of 2024?
answer:
Across the eight 2024 Beige Book editions, the overall assessment of economic activity remained anchored to "slight" or "modest" growth for most of the year, but the tone and breadth of that growth shifted in four distinct phases: cautious optimism in the first quarter (January–April), a turn toward heightened uncertainty in May, a broadening of flatness and weakness in the summer (July–September), and a modest rebound with improving sentiment in the final two editions (October–December).

### Chronological Evolution of the National Assessment

| Edition (Date) | Overall Activity Assessment | Key Descriptors & Tone | Notable Shifts vs. Prior Edition |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Jan 2024** [D13] | Majority reported little or no change; 3 modest growth, 1 moderate decline. | Cautious optimism; holiday spending a bright spot. | Baseline for 2024. Manufacturing broadly weaker; falling rate prospects cited as a source of optimism. |
| **Mar 2024** [D16] | Increased slightly, on balance; 8 slight-to-modest growth, 3 no change, 1 slight softening. | Generally positive outlook for next 6–12 months. | Consumer spending inched down; heightened price sensitivity/trade-down noted. Labor tightness eased further. |
| **Apr 2024** [D19] | Expanded slightly, on balance; 10 slight/modest growth (up from 8), 2 no change. | Cautiously optimistic. | Growth broadened (10 of 12 Districts growing). Home sales strengthened; manufacturing declined slightly. Wage growth returned to historical averages. |
| **May 2024** [D22] | Continued to expand; most slight/modest growth, 2 no change. | **Somewhat more pessimistic**; rising uncertainty and greater downside risks. | **Key tonal shift.** Retail spending flat-to-slightly-up; commercial real estate softened; hiring plans mixed. |
| **Jul 2024** [D25] | Maintained slight-to-modest growth in majority; 7 up, 5 flat/declining. | Uncertainty around election, policy, geopolitics, and inflation. | Breadth of growth narrowed: 5 Districts flat/declining (3 more than prior period). Expectations for slower growth over next 6 months. |
| **Sep 2024** [D27] | Grew slightly in only 3 Districts; **9 flat/declining** (up from 5). | Steady employment but firms more selective; consumer spending "ticked down." | **Marked softening.** Manufacturing declined in most Districts. Only 3 Districts anticipated slight declines, but broad flatness/weakness dominated. |
| **Oct 2024** [D29] | Little changed in nearly all Districts; 2 modest growth. | **Somewhat more optimistic** about longer-term outlook despite elevated uncertainty. | Sentiment improved. Loan demand improved on lower rates. Hurricane damage and dock strike caused minor disruptions. |
| **Dec 2024** [D31] | Rose slightly in most Districts; 3 modest/moderate growth, 2 flat/declining. | Optimism about rising demand; expectations for growth "rose moderately." | **Modest rebound.** Business contacts expressed optimism. Wage growth softened to modest pace. |

### Thematic Trends Across 2024

*   **Pace of Activity:** The Federal Reserve Districts consistently described activity as "slight" or "modest" throughout 2024, with no edition characterizing growth as "robust" or "strong." The primary variation was in the *breadth* of growth: from 10 of 12 Districts growing in April [D19] to only 3 growing in September [D27], before recovering to "most" Districts in December [D31].
*   **Labor Markets:** A steady cooling trend was evident across all eight editions. January noted "signs of a cooling labor market" [D13]; March reported "tightness eased further" [D16]; April saw wage growth "return to historical averages" [D19]; and by December, wage growth had "softened to a modest pace" [D31]. Employment levels remained generally flat to slightly up, with layoffs rare but hiring becoming more selective, particularly in the second half [D27][D29].
*   **Consumer Behavior:** Price sensitivity and "trading down" were persistent themes, first highlighted in March [D16] and continuing through December [D31]. Holiday spending in January was a notable positive outlier [D13], while retail spending was flat to slightly down in May [D22] and September [D27].
*   **Outlook and Uncertainty:** The tone shifted from optimism in Q1 (driven by expectations of falling rates [D13][D16]) to heightened pessimism and downside risk emphasis in May [D22] and July [D25]. By October, despite ongoing uncertainty, contacts became "somewhat more optimistic about the longer-term outlook" [D29], a sentiment that strengthened into December with business contacts expressing optimism about rising demand [D31]. Additionally, the December edition noted that businesses in several Districts indicated tariffs pose a significant upside risk to inflation [D32].

### Summary of the Arc
The 2024 Beige Book narrative began with cautious optimism and steady slight growth, deteriorated into a period of broadening flatness and heightened uncertainty in the summer (peaking in September with 9 of 12 Districts reporting flat or declining activity), and concluded with a modest rebound in activity and a notable improvement in forward-looking sentiment in the final two editions.

data.answer: Across the four first-half 2024 Beige Books, the national assessment of economic activity stayed broadly stable — slight-to-modest growth — but the tone shifted from cautious optimism in January to a more pessimistic, risk-aware outlook by May. In January, a majority of Districts reported little or no change, with three reporting modest growth and one a moderate decline; holiday consumer spending was a bright spot, manufacturing was broadly weaker, and the prospect of falling rates was a source of optimism [D13]. By March, activity had "increased slightly, on balance" (eight Districts slight-to-modest growth, three no change, one slight softening), with consumer spending inching down, heightened price sensitivity/trade-down, and a generally positive outlook for the next 6–12 months [D16]. In April, growth broadened — ten of twelve Districts reported slight or modest growth (up from eight) — with home sales strengthening and a "cautiously optimistic" outlook, though manufacturing declined slightly [D19]. By May, activity "continued to expand" but the outlook "grew somewhat more pessimistic amid reports of rising uncertainty and greater downside risks," with flat-to-slightly-up retail spending, softening commercial real estate, and mixed hiring plans [D22]. The key evolution: steady slight/modest growth throughout, labor markets cooling gradually, and a clear turn from optimism (Jan–Apr) to heightened uncertainty and downside-risk emphasis (May).
key_facts: Jan 2024: 'A majority of the twelve Federal Reserve Districts reported little or no change in economic activity... three reported modest growth and one reported a moderate decline.' Holiday spending met/exceeded expectations; manufacturing decreased in nearly all Districts; falling-rate prospects cited as optimism; most Districts' growth expectations positive or improved [D13].

Mar 2024: 'Economic activity increased slightly, on balance, since early January, with eight Districts reporting slight to modest growth... three others reporting no change, and one District noting a slight softening.' Consumer spending inched down; households trading down; outlook 'generally positive' for next 6–12 months [D16].

Apr 2024: 'Overall economic activity expanded slightly, on balance... Ten out of twelve Districts experienced either slight or modest economic growth—up from eight in the previous report.' Home sales strengthened in most Districts; manufacturing declined slightly; outlook 'cautiously optimistic, on balance' [D19].

May 2024: 'National economic activity continued to expand from early April to mid-May... Most Districts reported slight or modest growth, while two noted no change.' Retail spending flat to up slightly; commercial real estate softened; 'Overall outlooks grew somewhat more pessimistic amid reports of rising uncertainty and greater downside risks' [D22].

Labor markets cooled steadily across all four editions: Jan 'nearly all Districts cited one or more signs of a cooling labor market' [D13]; Mar 'tightness eased further' [D16]; Apr wage growth 'returned to their historical averages' [D19]; May wage growth 'at pre-pandemic historical averages or was normalizing' [D22].

data.answer:
Across the four second-half 2024 Beige Books, the national assessment of economic activity moved from "slight to modest growth" (July) to a clear broadening of flatness/decline (September), then to "little changed" with a more optimistic longer-term outlook (October), and finally to a modest rebound with "slight" growth in most Districts and rising expectations (December).

- July 2024 [D25]: Activity "maintained a slight to modest pace of growth in a majority of Districts," but five Districts reported flat or declining activity—three more than the prior period. Wages grew modestly to moderately; prices rose modestly; household spending was little changed. Expectations were for slower growth over the next six months due to election, policy, geopolitical, and inflation uncertainty.
- September 2024 [D27]: A marked softening—only three Districts reported slight growth, while flat/declining Districts rose from five to nine. Employment was steady (layoffs rare but firms more selective); consumer spending "ticked down" after holding steady; manufacturing declined in most Districts. Contacts generally expected activity to remain stable or improve somewhat, with three Districts anticipating slight declines.
- October 2024 [D29]: Activity was "little changed in nearly all Districts" since early September, with only two reporting modest growth; manufacturing continued to decline. Notably, despite elevated uncertainty, contacts were "somewhat more optimistic about the longer-term outlook." Loan demand improved on lower rates; hurricane damage and a brief dock strike caused minor disruptions.
- December 2024 [D31]: A modest rebound—activity "rose slightly in most Districts," with three regions showing modest/moderate growth offsetting flat/slightly declining activity in two. Growth was generally small, but expectations for growth "rose moderately" and business contacts expressed optimism about rising demand. Consumer spending was stable but with greater price/quality sensitivity; wage growth softened to a modest pace; tariffs were flagged as an upside inflation risk [D32].

Chronological arc: modest-but-uneven growth (July) → broadening weakness with nine flat/declining Districts (September) → flat but with improving sentiment (October) → slight broad-based recovery with stronger expectations (December).

September 2024: activity grew slightly in only three Districts; flat/declining Districts rose from five to nine; consumer spending 'ticked down'; manufacturing declined in most Districts [D27].

October 2024: activity 'little changed in nearly all Districts' since early September, two Districts with modest growth; 'Despite elevated uncertainty, contacts were somewhat more optimistic about the longer-term outlook' [D29].

December 2024: activity 'rose slightly in most Districts'; three regions modest/moderate growth offsetting two flat/declining; 'expectations for growth rose moderately across most geographies and sectors' [D31].
Wage growth trajectory: modest-to-moderate (July) → modest (Sept) → modest-to-moderate with slowing pace (Oct) → softened to modest (Dec) [D25][D27][D29][D31].
December prices: modest pace, input prices rising faster than selling prices compressing margins; tariffs cited as significant upside inflation risk [D32].

Across the eight 2024 Beige Book editions, the overall assessment of economic activity remained anchored to "slight" or "modest" growth for most of the year, but the tone and breadth of that growth shifted in three distinct phases: a period of cautious optimism in the first half (January–April), a turn toward heightened uncertainty and downside risks in May, a broadening of flatness and weakness in the second half (July–September), and a modest rebound with improving sentiment in the final two editions (October–December).

### Chronological Evolution of the National Assessment

| Edition (Date) | Overall Activity Assessment | Key Descriptors & Tone | Notable Shifts vs. Prior Edition |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |

| **Apr 2024** [D19] | Expanded slightly, on balance; 10 slight/modest growth (up from 8), 2 no change. | Cautiously optimistic. | Growth broadened (10 of 12 Districts growing). Home sales strengthened; manufacturing declined slightly. Wage growth returned to historical averages. |

| **Jul 2024** [D25] | Maintained slight-to-modest growth in majority; 7 up, 5 flat/declining. | Uncertainty around election, policy, geopolitics, and inflation. | Breadth of growth narrowed: 5 Districts flat/declining (3 more than prior period). Expectations for slower growth over next 6 months. |
| **Sep 2024** [D27] | Grew slightly in only 3 Districts; **9 flat/declining** (up from 5). | Steady employment but firms more selective; consumer spending "ticked down." | **Marked softening.** Manufacturing declined in most Districts. Only 3 Districts anticipated slight declines, but broad flatness/weakness dominated. |
| **Oct 2024** [D29] | Little changed in nearly all Districts; 2 modest growth. | **Somewhat more optimistic** about longer-term outlook despite elevated uncertainty. | Sentiment improved. Loan demand improved on lower rates. Hurricane damage and dock strike caused minor disruptions. |
| **Dec 2024** [D31] | Rose slightly in most Districts; 3 modest/moderate growth, 2 flat/declining. | Optimism about rising demand; expectations for growth "rose moderately." | **Modest rebound.** Business contacts expressed optimism. Wage growth softened to modest pace; tariffs flagged as upside inflation risk [D32]. |

### Thematic Trends Across 2024

*   **Pace of Activity:** The Federal Reserve Districts consistently described activity as "slight" or "modest" throughout 2024, with no edition characterizing growth as "robust" or "strong." The primary variation was in the *breadth* of growth: from 10 of 12 Districts growing in April [D19] to only 3 growing in September [D27], before recovering to "most" Districts in December [D31].
*   **Labor Markets:** A steady cooling trend was evident across all eight editions. January noted "signs of a cooling labor market" [D13]; March reported "tightness eased further" [D16]; April saw wage growth "return to historical averages" [D19]; and by December, wage growth had "softened to a modest pace" [D31]. Employment levels remained generally flat to slightly up, with layoffs rare but hiring becoming more selective, particularly in the second half [D27][D29].
*   **Consumer Behavior:** Price sensitivity and "trading down" were persistent themes, first highlighted in March [D16] and continuing through December [D31]. Holiday spending in January was a notable positive outlier [D13], while retail spending was flat to slightly down in May [D22] and September [D27].
*   **Outlook and Uncertainty:** The tone shifted from optimism in Q1 (driven by expectations of falling rates [D13][D16]) to heightened pessimism and downside risk emphasis in May [D22] and July [D25]. By October, despite ongoing uncertainty, contacts became "somewhat more optimistic about the longer-term outlook" [D29], a sentiment that strengthened into December with business contacts expressing optimism about rising demand [D31].

### Summary of the Arc
The 2024 Beige Book narrative began with cautious optimism and steady slight growth, deteriorated into a period of broadening flatness and heightened uncertainty in the summer (peaking in September with 9 of 12 Districts reporting flat or declining activity), and concluded with a modest rebound in activity and a notable improvement in forward-looking sentiment in the final two editions.

question: How did the Financial Stability Reports from May 2023 to May 2026 characterize asset valuations?
answer:
Across the Financial Stability Reports (FSRs) published from May 2023 through May 2026, the Federal Reserve consistently characterized asset valuations as elevated or high relative to fundamentals. The intensity of the language shifted from "moderate" in May 2023 to "notable" in October 2023 and April 2025, and "elevated" in the intervening and subsequent reports [D37][D19][D23][D26][D28][D32][D55]. The Fed repeatedly warned that these elevated valuations increase the possibility of outsized drops in asset prices, particularly given low liquidity in many markets [D2].

The evolution of these characterizations by asset class is detailed below:

### Equities
Equity valuations moved from being "above their historical median" in May 2023 to the "upper end of their historical distribution" by April 2024, a level they largely maintained through May 2026 [D50][D24][D43].
*   **May 2023:** Measures of equity prices relative to expected earnings were volatile but remained above their historical median [D50].
*   **October 2023:** Valuations increased modestly from an already high level; the forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio rose further above its historical median [D19][D20].
*   **April 2024:** The forward P/E ratio reached the upper end of its historical distribution since 1989; the equity premium stood well below its historical median [D24].
*   **November 2024:** The P/E ratio continued to climb toward the high end of its historical range; the equity premium remained well below average [D25][D27].
*   **April 2025:** Despite a >6% price decline in early April, equity prices remained high relative to forecasted earnings; the equity premium was near a 20-year low [D28][D46][D47].
*   **November 2025:** After recovering from April’s declines, the forward P/E ratio was once again close to the upper end of its historical range; the equity premium remained well below its historical median [D32][D44].
*   **May 2026:** The forward P/E ratio remained well above its historical median (though the associated figure caption noted it fell but stayed close to the upper end of its historical range); the equity premium moved up slightly from an overall low level [D34][D43].

### Corporate Credit
Corporate credit spreads were characterized as near historical averages in May 2023, then "low by historical standards" in most subsequent reports, with a brief widening to "moderate" levels in April 2025 [D37][D23][D25][D46][D34].
*   **May 2023:** Spreads were moderately lower, on net, and near their historical averages [D37].
*   **October 2023:** Spreads edged down and were somewhat below their historical averages [D19].
*   **April 2024:** Spreads narrowed to levels in the lower range of their historical distributions [D23].
*   **November 2024:** Spreads were low compared to their history [D25].
*   **April 2025:** Spreads widened notably from very compressed to moderate levels relative to their historical distributions, though they stayed at or below historical medians [D28][D46][D47].

The intensity of the language shifted from "moderate" in May 2023 to "notable" in October 2023 and April 2025, and "elevated" in the intervening and subsequent reports [D37][D19][D23][D26][D28][D32][D55]. The Fed repeatedly warned that these elevated valuations increase the possibility of outsized drops in asset prices, particularly given low liquidity in many markets [D2].

The evolution of these characterizations by asset class is detailed below:

### Equities
Equity valuations moved from being "above their historical median" in May 2023 to the "upper end of their historical distribution" by April 2024, a level they largely maintained through May 2026 [D50][D24][D43].
*   **May 2023:** Measures of equity prices relative to expected earnings were volatile but remained above their historical median [D50].
*   **October 2023:** Valuations increased modestly from an already high level; the forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio rose further above its historical median [D19][D20].
*   **April 2024:** The forward P/E ratio reached the upper end of its historical distribution since 1989; the equity premium stood well below its historical median [D24].
*   **November 2024:** The P/E ratio continued to climb toward the high end of its historical range; the equity premium remained well below average [D25][D27].
*   **April 2025:** Despite a >6% price decline in early April, equity prices remained high relative to forecasted earnings; the equity premium was near a 20-year low [D28][D46][D47].
*   **November 2025:** After recovering from April’s declines, the forward P/E ratio was once again close to the upper end of its historical range; the equity premium remained well below its historical median [D32][D44].
*   **May 2026:** The forward P/E ratio remained well above its historical median (though the associated figure caption noted it fell but stayed close to the upper end of its historical range); the equity premium moved up slightly from an overall low level [D34][D43].

### Corporate Credit
Corporate credit spreads were characterized as near historical averages in May 2023, then "low by historical standards" in most subsequent reports, with a brief widening to "moderate" levels in April 2025 [D37][D23][D25][D46][D34].
*   **May 2023:** Spreads were moderately lower, on net, and near their historical averages [D37].
*   **October 2023:** Spreads edged down and were somewhat below their historical averages [D19].
*   **April 2024:** Spreads narrowed to levels in the lower range of their historical distributions [D23].
*   **November 2024:** Spreads were low compared to their history [D25].
*   **April 2025:** Spreads widened notably from very compressed to moderate levels relative to their historical distributions, though they stayed at or below historical medians [D28][D46][D47].
*   **November 2025:** Spreads narrowed and stayed well below their historical medians [D32].
*   **May 2026:** Corporate bond and loan spreads remained low by historical standards, though leveraged loan spreads increased but stayed below median levels [D34][D55].

### Real Estate
Residential real estate valuations were described as "very elevated" or "near all-time highs" throughout the period, while commercial real estate (CRE) showed persistent weakness with declining prices and weak office fundamentals, though signs of stabilization emerged by 2025–2026 [D49][D37][D55].
*   **Residential:**
    *   **May 2023:** Valuations remained near all-time highs despite weakening activity and falling prices [D37][D49].
    *   **October 2023:** House prices started increasing again; prices relative to rents remained near all-time highs [D19].
    *   **April 2024:** Valuations remained near the peak levels seen in the mid-2000s [D23].
    *   **November 2024:** The ratio of house prices to rents was near the highest levels on record [D25].
    *   **April 2025:** Prices relative to fundamentals continued to be well above their historical averages [D57].
    *   **November 2025:** Prices continued to rise well above their historical relationship with fundamentals, but at a lower rate [D32].
    *   **May 2026:** Prices remained well above their historical relationship with fundamentals, even as house price growth slowed [D55].
*   **Commercial Real Estate (CRE):**
    *   **May 2023:** Valuations remained near historical highs even though price declines were widespread; fundamentals weakened, particularly for office [D37].
    *   **October 2023:** Rental income relative to property prices remained low; office fundamentals were especially weak with rising vacancy and slowing rent growth [D19].
    *   **April 2024:** Market conditions continued to deteriorate, especially for the office sector, with prices declining against high vacancy and weakening rents [D23].
    *   **November 2024:** Conditions continued to deteriorate, especially for office and multifamily; transaction-based price indexes were little changed, but rent growth slowed and vacancy rose [D25][D26].
    *   **April 2025:** The report noted CRE prices had declined, but did not explicitly detail the degree of stabilization in the asset valuation section summary, though it noted overall valuations were "notable" [D28].
    *   **November 2025:** Prices and fundamentals showed continued signs of stabilizing, though the potential for distressed sales remained if borrowers could not refinance [D32].
    *   **May 2026:** Prices and fundamentals showed continued signs of stabilizing, with the same caveat regarding refinancing risks [D55].

### Other Asset Classes
*   **Private Credit:** Not characterized in terms of valuation levels in the Asset Valuations section. Instead, it was discussed under Borrowing and Funding Risks. The November 2024 FSR noted rapid growth in private credit arrangements [D25]. The November 2025 FSR cited private credit opacity as a concern for potential negative spillovers [D40]. The May 2026 FSR included a dedicated box on private credit developments, noting that semi-liquid vehicles accounted for $425 billion in gross assets [D41].
*   **Crypto/Digital Assets:** Not characterized in terms of valuation levels in the Asset Valuations section. They were discussed under Funding Risks. The May 2023 FSR noted that stablecoins remained "structurally vulnerable to runs" and that their market capitalization had fallen 21% since the beginning of 2022 to $130 billion [D51]. The November 2024 FSR reiterated that stablecoins are structurally vulnerable to runs and lack a comprehensive federal prudential regulatory framework, while noting strong growth in recent years [D42].

| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **May 2023** | Moderate [D37] | Above historical median [D50] | Near historical averages [D37] | Very elevated / Near all-time highs [D49][D37] | Near historical highs; widespread price declines [D37] |
| **Oct 2023** | Notable [D19] | Increased modestly from high level [D19] | Somewhat below historical averages [D19] | Elevated relative to fundamentals; near all-time highs (price/rent) [D19] | Elevated relative to fundamentals; weak office fundamentals [D19] |
| **Apr 2024** | Elevated [D23] | Upper end of historical distribution [D24] | Lower range of historical distributions [D23] | Near peak levels seen in mid-2000s [D23] | Continued to deteriorate; prices declining [D23] |
| **Nov 2024** | Elevated [D26] | High end of historical range [D25] | Low compared to history [D25] | Near peak levels; price/rent near highest on record [D25][D26] | Little changed; slowing rent growth, rising vacancy [D25] |
| **Apr 2025** | Notable [D28] | High relative to earnings; near high end of range [D47] | Moderate levels (widened from compressed) [D46] | Well above historical averages [D57] | (Not explicitly detailed in valuation summary) [D28] |
| **Nov 2025** | Elevated [D32] | Close to upper end of historical range [D44] | Well below historical medians [D32] | Well above historical relationship with fundamentals [D32] | Continued signs of stabilizing [D32] |
| **May 2026** | Elevated [D55] | Well above historical median [D43] | Low by historical standards [D34] | Well above historical relationship with fundamentals [D55] | Continued signs of stabilizing [D55] |

question: How did FOMC participants' median projection for the 2026 unemployment rate change across the Summaries of Economic Projections from March 2025 to September 2026?
answer:
The FOMC participants' median projection for the 2026 unemployment rate ended the period 0.2 percentage points lower than where it started, moving from 4.3% in the March 2025 Summary of Economic Projections to 4.1% in the September 2026 SEP [D1]. The path was not monotonic: it first rose, then eased in two steps, with a flat stretch in between [D1].

| SEP release (meeting ending) | Median 2026 unemployment rate | Change vs. prior SEP |
|---|---|---|
| March 19, 2025 | 4.3% | — (baseline) |
| June 18, 2025 | 4.5% | +0.2 pp |
| September 17, 2025 | 4.4% | −0.1 pp |
| December 10, 2025 | 4.4% | 0.0 pp (flat) |
| March 18, 2026 | 4.4% | 0.0 pp (flat) |
| June 17, 2026 | 4.3% | −0.1 pp |
| September 16, 2026 | 4.1% | −0.2 pp |

All values are the median (50th percentile) of participants' projections for calendar-year 2026, as reported in each SEP's Table 1 [D1].

Step-by-step movement:
- March → June 2025: up 0.2 pp, from 4.3% to 4.5% [D1]
- June → September 2025: down 0.1 pp, to 4.4% [D1]
- September → December 2025: flat at 4.4% [D1]
- December 2025 → March 2026: flat at 4.4% [D1]
- March → June 2026: down 0.1 pp, to 4.3% [D1]
- June → September 2026: down 0.2 pp, to 4.1% [D1]

Net change from the March 2025 release to the September 2026 release: −0.2 percentage points (4.1% − 4.3%) [D1].

Note on coverage: the evidence covers exactly the seven SEP releases in the requested window (March 2025 through September 2026); no other releases are included or implied [D1].

question: Which Federal Reserve Governors gave speeches on stablecoins or tokenization in 2025 and 2026, and what was each one's main point?
answer:
Five Federal Reserve Governors—Christopher Waller, Michael Barr, Lisa Cook, Michelle Bowman, and Stephen Miran—gave speeches on stablecoins or tokenization between January 2025 and October 2026. Their views ranged from strongly pro-innovation (Waller, Bowman) to cautious and focused on financial stability risks (Barr, Cook), with Miran emphasizing the macroeconomic implications of stablecoin growth. Chairman Jerome Powell, as well as Governors Philip Jefferson, Adriana Kugler, and Kevin Warsh, did not deliver speeches substantively discussing these topics during this period [D1][D35][D38][D12][D9].

Here is a summary of each Governor's main points, organized by speaker:

### Christopher J. Waller
Waller was the most vocal advocate for embracing innovation, arguing that stablecoins are a legitimate form of private money that require a right-sized regulatory framework (specifically the GENIUS Act) and that the Fed should actively engage with tokenization and DeFi innovators.

*   **Feb 12, 2025 – "Reflections on a Maturing Stablecoin Market" (San Francisco):** Argued that stablecoins are private money subject to run risk and that the U.S. needs a clear, proportionate regulatory regime allowing both banks and non-banks to issue them. Noted that stablecoins account for over 80% of trading volume on major centralized crypto exchanges and ~99% of stablecoin market cap is dollar-denominated [D35][D3][D36][D37].
*   **Aug 20, 2025 – "Technological Advancements in Payments" (Wyoming Blockchain Symposium):** Described stablecoins as the latest private-sector payments innovation with the potential to extend the dollar's international role. Praised the GENIUS Act as an important step and stated the Fed is conducting technical research on tokenization, smart contracts, and AI, and should engage more with innovators [D10][D16][D33][D34].
*   **Sept 29, 2025 – "The Next Frontier of Payments Innovation" (Sibos, Frankfurt):** Framed stablecoins as "simply another choice" for consumers. Highlighted the "stablecoin sandwich" model and tokenized deposits as ways to improve cross-border payments, noting that GENIUS Act requirements (1:1 backing with safe liquid assets) address safety concerns [D54][D19][D55][D56].
*   **Oct 21, 2025 – "Embracing New Technologies and Players in Payments" (Federal Reserve Board, Washington, D.C.):** Welcomed the DeFi/crypto world into the payments conversation, stating the Fed is "welcoming" these players and conducting hands-on research on tokenization, smart contracts, and AI [D17][D44][D46].
*   **Feb 24, 2026 – "Operationalizing AI at the Federal Reserve" (FRB Boston):** Argued that tokenization, along with AI and quantum computing, is a frontier technology requiring a System-wide, coordinated Fed approach rather than Bank-by-Bank decisions [D52][D50].
*   **June 22, 2026 – "Welcoming Remarks on the International Role of the U.S. Dollar" (Washington, D.C.):** Stated that DLT and tokenized assets like stablecoins are creating new channels for global dollar intermediation, evolving the dollar's international role through both complement and competition with traditional finance [D14][D18].

### Michael S. Barr
Barr took the most cautious stance, emphasizing run risk, the quality of reserve assets, AML concerns, and gaps in the GENIUS Act. He consistently endorsed tokenized deposits as a safer alternative to stablecoins because they operate within the existing bank regulatory framework.

*   **Oct 16, 2025 – "Exploring the Possibilities and Risks of New Payment Technologies" (D.C. Fintech Week):** Acknowledged stablecoins' promise for near-real-time global payments but highlighted AML challenges due to their nature as bearer instruments on permissionless networks. Identified gaps in the GENIUS Act, including the use of uninsured deposits as reserves and trust-bank charter arbitrage. Endorsed tokenized deposits as a safer alternative because they benefit from deposit insurance and discount-window access [D43][D7][D42][D20][D41].
*   **March 31, 2026 – "Brief Remarks on Stablecoins" (The Federalist Society, Washington, D.C.):** Stated that while the GENIUS Act provides clarity, key concerns remain regarding AML/terrorist-financing risk and financial stability/run risk. Emphasized that stablecoins are stable only if reliably redeemable at par, and that issuers have incentives to stretch reserve-asset risk. Success depends on implementation details such as reserve asset quality, regulatory arbitrage, and consumer protection [D1][D30][D2].

### Lisa D. Cook
Cook framed both topics through a financial-stability lens, noting stablecoins' structural vulnerability to runs and tokenization's opportunities and challenges, while emphasizing the need for careful monitoring.

*   **Jan 6, 2025 – "An Assessment of the Economy and Financial Stability" (University of Michigan Law School):** Noted that stablecoins (~$170B AUM) have a small U.S. footprint and lack a comprehensive federal regulatory framework. Highlighted their structural vulnerability to runs, warning that liquidation of backing assets could be disruptive if linked to commercial paper or CD markets. Also raised questions about stablecoins' role in intermediation chains and as loan collateral [D38][D4][D39].
*   **May 8, 2026 – "Perspectives on Tokenization and Implications for the Financial System" (BCEAO Conference, Dakar, Senegal):** Defined tokenization as the digital representation of assets on DLT executed via smart contracts. Outlined benefits such as faster settlement, better recordkeeping, and improved cross-border payments, especially in emerging economies. Distinguished between directly-issued on-chain assets and tokenized representations of conventional assets. Supported innovation but stressed monitoring financial-stability implications, noting the Fed is researching tokenization but does not see it substituting for traditional market infrastructure [D26][D13][D11][D49].

### Michelle W. Bowman (Vice Chair for Supervision)
Bowman urged regulators to embrace tokenization and stablecoins rather than approach them with excessive caution, advocating for a tailored framework to keep the U.S. competitive.

*   **Aug 19, 2025 – "Embracing Innovation" (Wyoming Blockchain Symposium):** Argued that tokenization solves the friction of asset-ownership transfer (re-registration, escrow, timing), enabling faster and cheaper title transfer. Suggested a "tipping point" for broad adoption is possible and that banks of all sizes can benefit. Noted that the GENIUS Act has brought stablecoins to the forefront, positioning them as a fixture in the financial system. Called on regulators to depart from an overly cautious mindset and build a tailored framework that keeps the U.S. the best place to innovate [D12][D15][D31][D32].

### Stephen I. Miran
Miran focused on the macroeconomic and monetary policy implications of stablecoin growth, arguing they will become a multitrillion-dollar force.

*   **Nov 7, 2025 – "A Global Stablecoin Glut: Implications for Monetary Policy" (BCVC Summit, New York):** Argued that stablecoins are an established, fast-growing part of the financial landscape and a more efficient means of accessing dollars. Praised the GENIUS Act's 1:1 reserve requirement as its most important monetary-policy feature. Cited Fed staff-compiled private-sector estimates projecting stablecoin uptake of $1–3 trillion by the end of the decade, calling it a "multitrillion dollar elephant in the room" for central bankers. Noted that stablecoins could boost Treasury demand and affect loanable funds, with broad global adoption plausible, especially in emerging market economies with capital controls [D9][D5][D28][D27].

### Governors with No Relevant Speeches
*   **Jerome Powell (Chairman), Philip Jefferson, Adriana Kugler, and Kevin Warsh:** No speeches by these Governors in the collection substantively discuss stablecoins or tokenization during the Jan 2025–Oct 2026 period.

Six Federal Reserve Governors—Christopher Waller, Michael Barr, Lisa Cook, Michelle Bowman, and Stephen Miran—gave speeches on stablecoins or tokenization between January 2025 and October 2026. Their views ranged from strongly pro-innovation (Waller, Bowman) to cautious and focused on financial stability risks (Barr, Cook), with Miran emphasizing the macroeconomic implications of stablecoin growth. Chairman Kevin Warsh, as well as Governors Powell, Jefferson, and Kugler, did not deliver speeches substantively discussing these topics during this period [D1][D35][D38][D12][D9].

Here is a summary of each Governor's main points, organized by speaker:

### Christopher J. Waller
Waller was the most vocal advocate for embracing innovation, arguing that stablecoins are a legitimate form of private money that require a right-sized regulatory framework (specifically the GENIUS Act) and that the Fed should actively engage with tokenization and DeFi innovators.

*   **Feb 12, 2025 – "Reflections on a Maturing Stablecoin Market" (San Francisco):** Argued that stablecoins are private money subject to run risk and that the U.S. needs a clear, proportionate regulatory regime allowing both banks and non-banks to issue them. Noted that stablecoins account for over 80% of trading volume on major centralized crypto exchanges and ~99% of stablecoin market cap is dollar-denominated [D35][D3][D36][D37].
*   **Aug 20, 2025 – "Technological Advancements in Payments" (Wyoming Blockchain Symposium):** Described stablecoins as the latest private-sector payments innovation with the potential to extend the dollar's international role. Praised the GENIUS Act as an important step and stated the Fed is conducting technical research on tokenization, smart contracts, and AI, and should engage more with innovators [D10][D16][D33][D34].
*   **Sept 29, 2025 – "The Next Frontier of Payments Innovation" (Sibos, Frankfurt):** Framed stablecoins as "simply another choice" for consumers. Highlighted the "stablecoin sandwich" model and tokenized deposits as ways to improve cross-border payments, noting that GENIUS Act requirements (1:1 backing with safe liquid assets) address safety concerns [D54][D19][D55][D56].
*   **Oct 21, 2025 – "Embracing New Technologies and Players in Payments" (Federal Reserve Board, Washington, D.C.):** Welcomed the DeFi/crypto world into the payments conversation, stating the Fed is "welcoming" these players and conducting hands-on research on tokenization, smart contracts, and AI [D17][D44][D46].
*   **Feb 24, 2026 – "Operationalizing AI at the Federal Reserve" (FRB Boston):** Argued that tokenization, along with AI and quantum computing, is a frontier technology requiring a System-wide, coordinated Fed approach rather than Bank-by-Bank decisions [D52][D50].
*   **June 22, 2026 – "Welcoming Remarks on the International Role of the U.S. Dollar" (Washington, D.C.):** Stated that DLT and tokenized assets like stablecoins are creating new channels for global dollar intermediation, evolving the dollar's international role through both complement and competition with traditional finance [D14][D18].

### Michael S. Barr
Barr took the most cautious stance, emphasizing run risk, the quality of reserve assets, AML concerns, and gaps in the GENIUS Act. He consistently endorsed tokenized deposits as a safer alternative to stablecoins because they operate within the existing bank regulatory framework.

Fintech Week):** Acknowledged stablecoins' promise for near-real-time global payments but highlighted AML challenges due to their nature as bearer instruments on permissionless networks. Cook framed both topics through a financial-stability lens, noting stablecoins' structural vulnerability to runs and tokenization's opportunities and challenges, while emphasizing the need for careful monitoring.

Highlighted their structural vulnerability to runs, warning that liquidation of backing assets could be disruptive if linked to commercial paper or CD markets. Also raised questions about stablecoins' role in intermediation chains and as loan collateral [D38][D4][D39].
*   **May 8, 2026 – "Perspectives on Tokenization and Implications for the Financial System" (BCEAO Conference, Dakar, Senegal):** Defined tokenization as the digital representation of assets on DLT executed via smart contracts. Outlined benefits such as faster settlement, better recordkeeping, and improved cross-border payments, especially in emerging economies. Distinguished between directly-issued on-chain assets and tokenized representations of conventional assets. Supported innovation but stressed monitoring financial-stability implications, noting the Fed is researching tokenization but does not see it substituting for traditional market infrastructure [D26][D13][D11][D49].

### Michelle W. Bowman (Vice Chair for Supervision)
Bowman urged regulators to embrace tokenization and stablecoins rather than approach them with excessive caution, advocating for a tailored framework to keep the U.S. competitive.

Suggested a "tipping point" for broad adoption is possible and that banks of all sizes can benefit. Noted that the GENIUS Act has brought stablecoins to the forefront, positioning them as a fixture in the financial system. Called on regulators to depart from an overly cautious mindset and build a tailored framework that keeps the U.S. the best place to innovate [D12][D15][D31][D32].

### Stephen I. Miran
Miran focused on the macroeconomic and monetary policy implications of stablecoin growth, arguing they will become a multitrillion-dollar force.

Praised the GENIUS Act's 1:1 reserve requirement as its most important monetary-policy feature. Cited Fed staff-compiled private-sector estimates projecting stablecoin uptake of $1–3 trillion by the end of the decade, calling it a "multitrillion dollar elephant in the room" for central bankers. Noted that stablecoins could boost Treasury demand and affect loanable funds, with broad global adoption plausible, especially in emerging market economies with capital controls [D9][D5][D28][D27].

### Governors with No Relevant Speeches
*   **Kevin Warsh (Chairman):** His only speech in the collection during this period (Jackson Hole, Aug 28, 2026) focused on AI, forward guidance, and the economy; it did not substantively discuss stablecoins or tokenization.
*   **Jerome Powell, Philip Jefferson, and Adriana Kugler:** No speeches by these Governors in the collection substantively discuss stablecoins or tokenization during the Jan 2025–Oct 2026 period.

question: How did the Monetary Policy Reports from February 2025 to July 2026 describe the role of tariffs in inflation?
answer:
Taking "the Monetary Policy Reports" to mean the semi-annual reports to Congress, the three editions in the specified window are the February 7, 2025, June 20, 2025, and July 10, 2026 reports. Across them, the description of tariffs' role in inflation evolves from essentially absent (February 2025) to cautious and uncertain (June 2025) to a firmer, confirmed contribution that is now partially reversing (July 2026).

| Report (date) | How tariffs are described in relation to inflation | Magnitude | Duration / trajectory | Channels identified |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| February 7, 2025 | No analysis of tariff pass-through to domestic inflation. "Tariffs" appears only twice, in International Developments, in contexts unrelated to U.S. price inflation [D15][D16]. | Not assessed | Not assessed | Not assessed for inflation |
| June 20, 2025 | Effects on U.S. consumer prices are "highly uncertain, as trade policy continues to evolve, and it is still early to assess how consumers and firms will respond"; the pattern of goods price changes "suggests that tariffs may have contributed to the recent upturn in goods inflation" [D3]. | Qualitative only; no basis-point figure given | Not labeled temporary/transitory; "still early to assess" [D3] | Durable goods with high import content (household appliances, consumer electronics) saw "somewhat strong" price changes, while new motor vehicles did not; domestic steel/aluminum producer prices rose "substantially relative to the global prices... likely reflecting the effects of tariffs"; nonfuel import prices (which exclude tariffs) rose only modestly, implying foreign producers did not cut prices to U.S. importers; ISM and regional Fed surveys showed input prices "moved sharply higher" [D3]. |
| July 10, 2026 | Tariff increases "contributed in part to the upturn in consumer goods price increases" and "had pushed up domestic prices for some consumer goods"; tariffs are listed as one of three main drivers of higher measured prices (with the Middle East energy shock and AI-related demand) [D5][D6][D7]. | Qualitative only; no percentage-point pass-through figure; effects "cannot be observed directly in the official consumer price statistics" [D5] | A 2025 ("last year") phenomenon, now partially reversed: a February 2026 Supreme Court ruling invalidated many prevailing tariff measures, lowering the average U.S. tariff rate (only partially offset by new alternative measures), so import prices paid by domestic producers (which include tariffs) "are estimated to have decreased this year" [D8]. | Concentrated in high-import-content goods (household appliances, consumer electronics) and food; AI-related high-tech goods largely tariff-exempt; food price step-up attributed in part to "the effects of higher tariffs and increases in agricultural and livestock commodity prices"; tariffs also weighed on consumer spending via real disposable income [D5][D9][D13]. |

Supporting detail by edition:

- February 7, 2025 report: The inflation discussion attributes 2024 dynamics to core services, housing, and "a small boost" from nonfuel import prices (up 2.4 percent over the year), without connecting import prices to tariffs [D32]. The Summary reports PCE inflation of 2.6 percent and core PCE of 2.8 percent over the 12 months ending December 2024, with inflation "somewhat above 2 percent" [D2][D64]. The two tariff mentions are: (1) "the prospect of new U.S. tariffs on EME exports to the U.S." cited as a factor behind large fourth-quarter 2024 outflows from emerging market funds (p. 47) [D15]; and (2) "potential increases in U.S. tariffs on imports" cited by some market participants as a factor pushing the broad dollar index higher (pp. 47-48) [D16]. The Summary of Economic Projections' risk-weighting diffusion indexes for core PCE inflation show "weighted to upside" versus "broadly balanced" assessments, with no tariff attribution (pp. 70-73) [D22][D58]. In short, this edition does not analyze tariff pass-through to inflation.

- June 20, 2025 report: The core language is deliberately cautious. The report states that "the effects on U.S. consumer prices of the increase in import tariffs this year are highly uncertain, as trade policy continues to evolve, and it is still early to assess how consumers and firms will respond," while noting that "the pattern of net price changes among goods categories this year suggests that tariffs may have contributed to the recent upturn in goods inflation," with "somewhat strong" price changes in household appliances and consumer electronics but not in new motor vehicles (p. 17) [D3]. On channels, it reports that prices received by domestic producers of steel and aluminum "have risen substantially relative to the global prices, on net, over this period, likely reflecting the effects of tariffs," and that nonfuel import prices (which exclude tariffs) "have increased modestly so far this year, suggesting foreign producers have not responded materially to the higher tariffs by reducing the prices they charge U.S. importers," while ISM and regional Fed surveys show input prices "moved sharply higher this year" (p. 17) [D3]. The Summary notes household and business sentiment declined "amid concerns about the effects of higher tariffs on inflation and employment" (p. 11) [D23], and the Domestic Developments section flags "some early signs that higher tariffs on U.S. goods imports are pushing up prices for some consumer goods" (p. 15) [D26]. The report cites two recent analyses for detecting tariff effects in real time: Minton & Somale (2025), "Detecting Tariff Effects on Consumer Prices in Real Time" (FEDS Notes, May 9), and Cavallo, Llamas & Vazquez (2025), "Tracking the Short-Run Price Impact of U.S. Tariffs" (working paper, June 3) (p. 17, footnote 2) [D4]. On expectations, longer-term measures "remain well anchored" (SPF median 2.0 percent for the five years beginning five years out), while the Michigan 12-month median rose from 2.8 percent (December) to 5.1 percent (June), "with almost two-thirds of respondents citing tariff-related concerns," and the Michigan 5-10 year median climbed from 3 percent to 4.1 percent (pp. 19-20) [D35][D45]. The report also links a Q1 GDP pause to "a historic surge in imports that likely reflects a pull-forward of purchases of goods from abroad by households and businesses ahead of expected increases in tariffs," with real imports surging at a 43 percent annual rate in Q1 and goods imports falling sharply in April after many tariffs were raised (pp. 28, 34) [D39][D61], and notes business sentiment and capital spending plans fell "over concerns about tariffs and the rise in uncertainty" (pp. 32-33) [D65]. It does not assign a specific quantitative magnitude to the pass-through or label the effect as temporary/transitory.

- July 10, 2026 report: The language is firmer than in June 2025. The Summary lists "earlier tariff hikes that pushed up domestic prices of some imported goods" as one of three factors "contributing to higher measured prices," alongside the Middle East energy shock and AI-related demand (pp. 9-10) [D7]. The Domestic Developments section states that "measures of consumer price inflation moved up steadily over the remainder of last year amid signs that increases in tariffs on U.S. goods imports had pushed up domestic prices for some consumer goods," with PCE rising 4.1 percent and core PCE 3.4 percent over the 12 months ending May 2026 (p. 13) [D6]. On the core goods channel, it notes that "the pattern of price changes last year suggests that tariff increases contributed in part to the upturn in consumer goods price increases," with higher monthly price increases in high-import-content categories such as household appliances and consumer electronics, while adding that "most of these products [high-tech goods] are exempt from tariffs, so changes in tariff rates are not an important factor in their prices" (p. 15) [D5]. Food prices: "A few somewhat interrelated factors contributing to the step-up in measured food price inflation include the effects of higher tariffs and increases in agricultural and livestock commodity prices" (p. 14) [D9]. On duration/reversal, it reports that import prices paid by domestic producers, which include tariffs, "are estimated to have decreased this year... primarily reflect a decline in the average U.S. tariff rate following February's Supreme Court ruling that invalidated many prevailing tariff measures and whose repeal was only partially offset by new, alternative tariff measures" (p. 16) [D8]. Tariffs also weighed on consumer spending via real disposable income (pp. 27-28) [D13], and on foreign activity, with "U.S. sectoral tariffs continuing to weigh on manufacturing" in Mexico and Canada (p. 41) [D40]. The FOMC's policy context notes inflation "remains elevated relative to the Committee's 2 percent goal, in part reflecting supply shocks that have driven price increases in certain sectors, including energy" (pp. 11-12) [D10]. On expectations, the Michigan 12-month measure rose from 3.4 percent (February) to 4.6 percent (June 2026), "an elevated rate that was nevertheless still well below the peak that followed last year's announcements of tariff increases" (p. 18) [D12]. Like the June 2025 edition, this report provides no numeric pass-through estimate (no percentage-point figure).

Evolution across the three editions: The February 2025 report contains no tariff-inflation analysis at all [D15][D16][D32]. The June 2025 report introduces the topic with hedged language ("highly uncertain," "may have contributed," "still early to assess") and identifies specific channels (durable goods, steel/aluminum, input costs) but no magnitude or duration label [D3][D26][D23]. The July 2026 report confirms the contribution in firmer terms ("contributed in part," "had pushed up domestic prices"), adds the food channel and the AI-goods carve-out, and describes the effect as a 2025 phenomenon now partially reversed following the February 2026 Supreme Court ruling [D5][D6][D7][D8][D9]. None of the three editions assigns a specific quantitative (basis-point or percentage-point) magnitude to the tariff pass-through; all describe it qualitatively.

data.answer: The February 7, 2025 Monetary Policy Report (fed_monetary_policy_report_2025-02-07) contains no dedicated discussion of the impact of tariffs on inflation, and no language describing the magnitude, duration, or channels of tariff pass-through to prices. The word "tariffs" appears only twice, in the International Developments section, in contexts unrelated to domestic inflation pass-through: (1) the "prospect of new U.S. tariffs on EME exports to the U.S." is cited as a factor behind large fourth-quarter outflows from emerging market funds (p. 47) [D15], and (2) "potential increases in U.S. tariffs on imports" is cited as one factor some market participants pointed to in explaining the recent rise in the broad dollar index (pp. 47-48) [D16]. The report's inflation discussion (Summary, p. 11 [D2][D64]; Domestic Developments, pp. 15-18 [D32]) attributes 2024 inflation dynamics to core services, housing, and a "small boost" from nonfuel import prices (up 2.4 percent over the year, figure 6) [D32], but does not connect import prices to tariffs. The SEP section reports participants' risk assessments for core PCE inflation (e.g., "weighted to upside" vs. "broadly balanced" diffusion indexes, pp. 70-73 [D22][D58]) without attributing any risk to tariffs. In short, as of February 7, 2025, the MPR did not analyze tariff pass-through to inflation; that analysis appears in later editions (e.g., the June 2025 MPR).

The task's premise (that this MPR discusses tariff pass-through to inflation) is not supported by the document; the detailed tariff-inflation analysis appears in the June 2025 MPR, which is outside the scope of this task.

data.answer: The July 10, 2026 Monetary Policy Report (fed_monetary_policy_report_2026-07-10) discusses tariff effects on inflation in the Summary (pp. 9-10), the Domestic Developments inflation section (pp. 13-16), the consumer spending discussion (pp. 27-28), and International Developments (pp. 41-42). The report's core finding: tariff increases in 2025 "contributed in part to the upturn in consumer goods price increases," with pass-through concentrated in high-import-content goods (household appliances, consumer electronics) and food, while AI-related high-tech goods were largely tariff-exempt. The report does NOT provide a numeric pass-through estimate (no percentage-point figure); it describes the effect qualitatively, noting tariff effects "cannot be observed directly in the official consumer price statistics" and "depend on the responses of consumers, firms, importers, and foreign exporters." Duration: the tariff-driven price increases are described as a 2025 phenomenon ("last year") that has since been partially reversed — a February 2026 Supreme Court ruling invalidated many prevailing tariff measures, lowering the average U.S. tariff rate (only partially offset by new alternative measures), so import prices paid by domestic producers (which include tariffs) "are estimated to have decreased this year." Evolution: the June 2025 MPR called the effects "highly uncertain" and "still early to assess," with tariffs "may have contributed" to goods inflation; by July 2026 the language is firmer ("contributed in part," "had pushed up domestic prices"), and tariffs are now listed as one of three main drivers of higher measured prices (alongside the Middle East energy shock and AI demand). The FOMC's June 2026 statement attributes elevated inflation partly to "supply shocks that have driven price increases in certain sectors, including energy," and the report notes tariffs also weighed on consumer spending via real disposable income and on foreign activity (Mexico, Canada manufacturing).

data.answer: The June 20, 2025 Monetary Policy Report discusses tariff effects on inflation primarily in the "Inflation has continued to ease" section of Domestic Developments (pp. 15-20), with supporting mentions in the Summary (p. 11), the GDP/imports discussion (pp. 28, 34), business sentiment (pp. 32-33), and International Developments (pp. 42-43). On channels, the report notes (1) domestic steel/aluminum producer prices rose "substantially relative to the global prices, on net... likely reflecting the effects of tariffs"; (2) nonfuel import prices (which exclude tariffs) rose only modestly, "suggesting foreign producers have not responded materially to the higher tariffs by reducing the prices they charge U.S. importers"; and (3) firms widely report input cost pressures "sharply higher" in ISM and regional Fed surveys. Across them, the description of tariffs' role in inflation evolves from essentially absent (February 2025) to cautious and uncertain (June 2025) to a firmer, confirmed contribution that is now partially reversing (July 2026).

|---|---|---|---|---|
| February 7, 2025 | No analysis of tariff pass-through to domestic inflation. "Tariffs" appears only twice, in International Developments, in contexts unrelated to U.S. price inflation [D15][D16]. | Not assessed | Not assessed | Not assessed for inflation |
| June 20, 2025 | Effects on U.S. consumer prices are "highly uncertain, as trade policy continues to evolve, and it is still early to assess how consumers and firms will respond"; the pattern of goods price changes "suggests that tariffs may have contributed to the recent upturn in goods inflation" [D3]. | Qualitative only; no basis-point figure given | Not labeled temporary/transitory; "still early to assess" [D3] | Durable goods with high import content (household appliances, consumer electronics) saw "somewhat strong" price changes, while new motor vehicles did not; domestic steel/aluminum producer prices rose "substantially relative to the global prices... likely reflecting the effects of tariffs"; nonfuel import prices (which exclude tariffs) rose only modestly, implying foreign producers did not cut prices to U.S. importers; ISM and regional Fed surveys showed input prices "moved sharply higher" [D3]. |

- February 7, 2025 report: The inflation discussion attributes 2024 dynamics to core services, housing, and "a small boost" from nonfuel import prices (up 2.4 percent over the year), without connecting import prices to tariffs [D32]. The Summary reports PCE inflation of 2.6 percent and core PCE of 2.8 percent over the 12 months ending December 2024, with inflation "somewhat above 2 percent" [D2][D64]. The two tariff mentions are: (1) "the prospect of new U.S. tariffs on EME exports to the U.S." cited as a factor behind large fourth-quarter 2024 outflows from emerging market funds (p. 47) [D15]; and (2) "potential increases in U.S. tariffs on imports" cited by some market participants as a factor pushing the broad dollar index higher (pp. 47-48) [D16]. The Summary of Economic Projections' risk-weighting diffusion indexes for core PCE inflation show "weighted to upside" versus "broadly balanced" assessments, with no tariff attribution (pp. 70-73) [D22][D58]. In short, this edition does not analyze tariff pass-through to inflation.

- June 20, 2025 report: The core language is deliberately cautious. The report states that "the effects on U.S. consumer prices of the increase in import tariffs this year are highly uncertain, as trade policy continues to evolve, and it is still early to assess how consumers and firms will respond," while noting that "the pattern of net price changes among goods categories this year suggests that tariffs may have contributed to the recent upturn in goods inflation," with "somewhat strong" price changes in household appliances and consumer electronics but not in new motor vehicles (p. 17) [D3]. On channels, it reports that prices received by domestic producers of steel and aluminum "have risen substantially relative to the global prices, on net, over this period, likely reflecting the effects of tariffs," and that nonfuel import prices (which exclude tariffs) "have increased modestly so far this year, suggesting foreign producers have not responded materially to the higher tariffs by reducing the prices they charge U.S. importers," while ISM and regional Fed surveys show input prices "moved sharply higher this year" (p. 17) [D3]. The Summary notes household and business sentiment declined "amid concerns about the effects of higher tariffs on inflation and employment" (p. 11) [D23], and the Domestic Developments section flags "some early signs that higher tariffs on U.S. goods imports are pushing up prices for some consumer goods" (p. 15) [D26]. The report also links a Q1 GDP pause to "a historic surge in imports that likely reflects a pull-forward of purchases of goods from abroad by households and businesses ahead of expected increases in tariffs," with real imports surging at a 43 percent annual rate in Q1 and goods imports falling sharply in April after many tariffs were raised (pp. 28, 34) [D39][D61], and notes business sentiment and capital spending plans fell "over concerns about tariffs and the rise in uncertainty" (pp. 32-33) [D65]. It does not assign a specific quantitative magnitude to the pass-through or label the effect as temporary/transitory.

- July 10, 2026 report: The language is firmer than in June 2025. The Summary lists "earlier tariff hikes that pushed up domestic prices of some imported goods" as one of three factors "contributing to higher measured prices," alongside the Middle East energy shock and AI-related demand (pp. 9-10) [D7]. The Domestic Developments section states that "measures of consumer price inflation moved up steadily over the remainder of last year amid signs that increases in tariffs on U.S. goods imports had pushed up domestic prices for some consumer goods," with PCE rising 4.1 percent and core PCE 3.4 percent over the 12 months ending May 2026 (p. 13) [D6]. On the core goods channel, it notes that "the pattern of price changes last year suggests that tariff increases contributed in part to the upturn in consumer goods price increases," with higher monthly price increases in high-import-content categories such as household appliances and consumer electronics, while adding that "most of these products [high-tech goods] are exempt from tariffs, so changes in tariff rates are not an important factor in their prices" (p. 15) [D5]. Food prices: "A few somewhat interrelated factors contributing to the step-up in measured food price inflation include the effects of higher tariffs and increases in agricultural and livestock commodity prices" (p. 14) [D9]. On duration/reversal, it reports that import prices paid by domestic producers, which include tariffs, "are estimated to have decreased this year... primarily reflect a decline in the average U.S. tariff rate following February's Supreme Court ruling that invalidated many prevailing tariff measures and whose repeal was only partially offset by new, alternative tariff measures" (p. 16) [D8]. Tariffs also weighed on consumer spending via real disposable income (pp. 27-28) [D13], and on foreign activity, with "U.S. sectoral tariffs continuing to weigh on manufacturing" in Mexico and Canada (p. 41) [D40]. The FOMC's policy context notes inflation "remains elevated relative to the Committee's 2 percent goal, in part reflecting supply shocks that have driven price increases in certain sectors, including energy" (pp. 11-12) [D10]. On expectations, the Michigan 12-month measure rose from 3.4 percent (February) to 4.6 percent (June 2026), "an elevated rate that was nevertheless still well below the peak that followed last year's announcements of tariff increases" (p. 18) [D12]. Like the June 2025 edition, this report provides no numeric pass-through estimate (no percentage-point figure).

Evolution across the three editions: The February 2025 report contains no tariff-inflation analysis at all [D15][D16][D32]. The June 2025 report introduces the topic with hedged language ("highly uncertain," "may have contributed," "still early to assess") and identifies specific channels (durable goods, steel/aluminum, input costs) but no magnitude or duration label [D3][D26][D23]. The July 2026 report confirms the contribution in firmer terms ("contributed in part," "had pushed up domestic prices"), adds the food channel and the AI-goods carve-out, and describes the effect as a 2025 phenomenon now partially reversed following the February 2026 Supreme Court ruling [D5][D6][D7][D8][D9]. None of the three editions assigns a specific quantitative (basis-point or percentage-point) magnitude to the tariff pass-through; all describe it qualitatively.

question: What changes to the Federal Reserve Board's membership and leadership happened between January 2025 and September 2026?
answer:
Between January 2025 and September 2026, the Federal Reserve Board of Governors experienced a complete turnover of its top leadership and several changes in membership. The most significant shift was the transition of the Chair from Jerome Powell to Kevin Warsh in May 2026. Additionally, the Vice Chair for Supervision role changed from Michael Barr to Michelle Bowman in mid-2025, and the Board’s membership was altered by the resignation of Adriana Kugler, the appointment and subsequent resignation of Stephen Miran, and the appointment of Kevin Warsh.

**Correction on Vice Chair Leadership:**
Contrary to the initial draft, **John C. Williams** served as Vice Chair during the latter part of this period, not Philip Jefferson. FOMC minutes from the June 17, 2026, and July 29, 2026, meetings explicitly list John C. Williams as Vice Chair [D31][D48]. While Philip Jefferson is identified as Vice Chair in a January 2026 speech [W61] and an October 2026 speech [W67], the FOMC attendance records for the period immediately following the Chair transition (June and July 2026) confirm Williams held the title. The evidence does not specify the exact date of the transition between Jefferson and Williams, but it occurred between January 2026 and June 2026.

**Correction on Susan Collins and Austan Goolsbee:**
The claim that Susan Collins and Austan Goolsbee transitioned from Board members to Reserve Bank Presidents effective March 1, 2026, is not supported by the provided evidence. The FOMC minutes show a change in their listed roles between the September 17, 2025, meeting (where they are listed as Board members) and the March 18, 2026, meeting (where they are listed as Reserve Bank Presidents of Boston and Chicago, respectively) [D13][D16]. However, no document in the evidence specifies an "effective March 1, 2026" date or confirms the direction of the move as a departure from the Board to a Reserve Bank presidency; it only documents the change in their FOMC attendance status.

Here is the chronological summary of the confirmed changes:

| Date | Individual | Change in Role/Status | Details |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Jan 6, 2025** | **Michael Barr** | Announced step-down as Vice Chair for Supervision | Effective Feb 28, 2025; continued serving as a Governor [D3][W21]. |
| **Feb 28, 2025** | **Michael Barr** | Stepped down as Vice Chair for Supervision | Remained a Governor [D3][W21]. |
| **Jun 9, 2025** | **Michelle Bowman** | Sworn in as Vice Chair for Supervision | Succeeded Barr; nominated Mar 24, 2025, confirmed Jun 4, 2025 [D9][W39][W40]. |
| **Aug 8, 2025** | **Adriana Kugler** | Resigned as Governor | Served since Sep 13, 2023; returned to Georgetown University [D1][W32]. |
| **Sep 16, 2025** | **Stephen Miran** | Sworn in as Governor | Filled Kugler’s unexpired term ending Jan 31, 2026; nominated Sep 2, 2025, confirmed Sep 15, 2025 [D6][W2]. |
| **May 12, 2026** | **Kevin Warsh** | Confirmed as Governor | Senate vote 51-45; term ends Jan 31, 2040 [D8][W7]. |
| **May 13, 2026** | **Kevin Warsh** | Confirmed as Chairman | Senate vote 54-45 [D8][W49]. |
