data.answer: Across the 14 FOMC statements from January 29, 2025 through September 16, 2026, the federal funds target range moved from 4-1/4 to 4-1/2 percent (held Jan–Jul 2025) down to 3-1/2 to 3-3/4 percent after three 25bp cuts (Sep, Oct, Dec 2025), then held at 3-1/2 to 3-3/4 percent for five consecutive meetings (Jan–Jul 2026), before a 25bp HIKE to 3-3/4 to 4 percent on September 16, 2026 — the first rate increase of this cycle. Key turning points: (1) September 17, 2025 — first cut, justified by "the shift in the balance of risks" with "downside risks to employment" rising, as the statement noted "Inflation has moved up and remains somewhat elevated"; (2) October 29, 2025 — second cut plus a decision to conclude the balance-sheet runoff on December 1, 2025; (3) December 10, 2025 — third cut plus a new commitment to "initiate purchases of shorter-term Treasury securities as needed to maintain an ample supply of reserves"; (4) April 29, 2026 — inflation language hardened from "somewhat elevated" to "elevated, in part reflecting the recent increase in global energy prices," with Middle East developments cited; (5) June 17, 2026 — the statement was completely rewritten into a much shorter format (dropping the "extent and timing of additional adjustments" easing-bias language and the "strongly committed to supporting maximum employment and returning inflation to its 2 percent objective" sentence), adding "The Committee will deliver price stability" and "reaffirmed its policy of maintaining ample reserves"; (6) September 16, 2026 — the first hike, with the statement saying "Today's policy action will support a timelier return to the Committee's 2 percent goal." Notably, in July 2026 three dissenters (Hammack, Kashkari, Logan) preferred to RAISE the rate, and in April 2026 three dissenters objected to an "easing bias" in the statement.
key_facts: Jan 29, 2025: HOLD at 4-1/4 to 4-1/2%; 'risks to achieving its employment and inflation goals are roughly in balance'; 'Inflation remains somewhat elevated'; continuing QT [D136].

Mar 19, 2025: HOLD at 4-1/4 to 4-1/2%; 'Uncertainty around the economic outlook has increased'; QT pace slowed — Treasury redemption cap cut from $25B to $5B beginning April, agency cap kept at $35B; Waller dissented (preferred to continue current QT pace) [D137].
May 7, 2025: HOLD at 4-1/4 to 4-1/2%; 'Uncertainty about the economic outlook has increased further'; 'judges that the risks of higher unemployment and higher inflation have risen' [D138].
Jun 18, 2025: HOLD at 4-1/4 to 4-1/2%; 'Uncertainty about the economic outlook has diminished but remains elevated' [D139].
Jul 30, 2025: HOLD at 4-1/4 to 4-1/2%; 'growth of economic activity moderated in the first half of the year'; Bowman and Waller dissented, preferring a 25bp cut [D140].

Sep 17, 2025: CUT 25bp to 4 to 4-1/4%; 'in light of the shift in the balance of risks'; 'Inflation has moved up and remains somewhat elevated'; 'downside risks to employment have risen'; Miran dissented preferring a 50bp cut [D141].

Oct 29, 2025: CUT 25bp to 3-3/4 to 4%; 'Inflation has moved up since earlier in the year and remains somewhat elevated'; 'decided to conclude the reduction of its aggregate securities holdings on December 1'; Miran (50bp cut) and Schmid (hold) dissented [D142].

Dec 10, 2025: CUT 25bp to 3-1/2 to 3-3/4%; 'reserve balances have declined to ample levels and will initiate purchases of shorter-term Treasury securities as needed to maintain an ample supply of reserves'; Miran (50bp cut), Goolsbee and Schmid (hold) dissented [D143].
Jan 28, 2026: HOLD at 3-1/2 to 3-3/4%; 'Job gains have remained low, and the unemployment rate has shown some signs of stabilization'; Miran and Waller dissented preferring a 25bp cut [D144].
Mar 18, 2026: HOLD at 3-1/2 to 3-3/4%; first mention of Middle East: 'The implications of developments in the Middle East for the U.S. economy are uncertain'; Miran dissented (25bp cut) [D145].

Apr 29, 2026: HOLD at 3-1/2 to 3-3/4%; inflation language shifted to 'Inflation is elevated, in part reflecting the recent increase in global energy prices'; 'Developments in the Middle East are contributing to a high level of uncertainty'; Hammack, Kashkari and Logan dissented, objecting to 'inclusion of an easing bias in the statement' [D146].

Jun 17, 2026: HOLD at 3-1/2 to 3-3/4%, 12-0 vote; statement rewritten into a much shorter format: 'reaffirmed its policy of maintaining ample reserves in the banking system'; 'Inflation remains elevated relative to the Committee's 2 percent goal, in part reflecting supply shocks that have driven price increases in certain sectors, including energy. The Committee will deliver price stability.' [D147].

Jul 29, 2026: HOLD at 3-1/2 to 3-3/4%, 9-3 vote; Hammack, Kashkari and Logan dissented, preferring to RAISE the target range by 25bp; 'The Committee is continuing its policy of maintaining ample reserves' [D155].
Sep 16, 2026: HIKE 25bp to 3-3/4 to 4 percent, 12-0 vote; 'Today's policy action will support a timelier return to the Committee's 2 percent goal. The Committee will deliver price stability.' [D156].

data.text: I now have the full text of all 17 FOMC statements from February 2023 through December 2024. Let me compile the findings.

data.answer:
Across the 17 FOMC statements from the Feb 1, 2023 meeting through the Dec 18, 2024 meeting, the federal funds target range moved from 4-1/2 to 4-3/4 percent (start of period) up to a peak of 5-1/4 to 5-1/2 percent (reached May 2023), held there for 11 consecutive meetings (June 2023–July 2024), then was cut 50 bps in September 2024 to 4-3/4 to 5 percent, and cut 25 bps each in November and December 2024, ending at 4-1/4 to 4-1/2 percent. The period thus captures the tail end of the hiking cycle (Feb, Mar, May, Jul 2023), a long pause (Jun 2023–Jul 2024), and the start of the easing cycle (Sep, Nov, Dec 2024).

Key turning points: (1) Hiking continued into 2023 — the Feb 1, 2023 statement raised the range to 4-1/2 to 4-3/4 percent and still "anticipates that ongoing increases...will be appropriate" [D128]; March 22, 2023 raised it to 4-3/4 to 5 percent [D129]; May 3, 2023 raised it to 5 to 5-1/4 percent [D130]; and July 26, 2023 raised it to the peak 5-1/4 to 5-1/2 percent [D132]. (2) The pause began June 14, 2023, when the Committee "decided to maintain the target range...at 5 to 5-1/4 percent," explicitly noting that holding steady "allows the Committee to assess additional information" [D131]; the range was then held at 5-1/4 to 5-1/2 percent from September 2023 through July 2024 [D133, D134, D135, D157, D158, D159, D160, D161]. (3) The easing cycle began September 18, 2024, with a 50 bps cut to 4-3/4 to 5 percent, justified by the Committee having "gained greater confidence that inflation is moving sustainably toward 2 percent" [D162]; this was followed by 25 bps cuts in November 7, 2024 (to 4-1/2 to 4-3/4 percent) [D163] and December 18, 2024 (to 4-1/4 to 4-1/2 percent) [D164].

Notable language evolution: Inflation language softened gradually from "Inflation remains elevated" (through Nov 2023) to "Inflation has eased over the past year but remains elevated" (Dec 2023–Jun 2024), then to "remains somewhat elevated" (Jul–Dec 2024), and finally to "Inflation has made further progress toward the Committee's 2 percent objective but remains somewhat elevated" (Sep–Dec 2024) [D135, D157, D161, D162]. The risk framing shifted from "highly attentive to inflation risks" (2023–Jun 2024) to "attentive to the risks to both sides of its dual mandate" (from Jul 2024) [D161], and the risk balance moved from "moving into better balance" (Jan–Mar 2024) to "roughly in balance" (Sep–Dec 2024) [D157, D162]. The March 2023 statement introduced the "U.S. banking system is sound and resilient" language (post-SVB) [D129], and the Feb 2023 statement was the last to reference Russia's war against Ukraine [D128]. On the balance sheet, the May 1, 2024 statement announced a slowdown in QT, reducing the monthly Treasury redemption cap from $60 billion to $25 billion beginning in June while keeping the agency cap at $35 billion [D159]. The "strongly committed to returning inflation to its 2 percent objective" language was replaced in September 2024 with "strongly committed to supporting maximum employment and returning inflation to its 2 percent objective" [D162].
key_facts: Feb 1, 2023: HIKE to 4-1/2 to 4-3/4 percent; 'anticipates that ongoing increases in the target range will be appropriate'; last statement to reference Russia's war against Ukraine [D128].
Mar 22, 2023: HIKE to 4-3/4 to 5 percent; introduced 'U.S. banking system is sound and resilient' language [D129].
May 3, 2023: HIKE to 5 to 5-1/4 percent [D130].
Jun 14, 2023: HOLD at 5 to 5-1/4 percent — first hold of the period; 'Holding the target range steady at this meeting allows the Committee to assess additional information' [D131].
Jul 26, 2023: HIKE to 5-1/4 to 5-1/2 percent (peak) [D132].
Sep 20, 2023: HOLD at 5-1/4 to 5-1/2 percent [D133].
Nov 1, 2023: HOLD at 5-1/4 to 5-1/2 percent [D134].
Dec 13, 2023: HOLD at 5-1/4 to 5-1/2 percent; inflation language shifts to 'has eased over the past year but remains elevated' [D135].

Jan 31, 2024: HOLD at 5-1/4 to 5-1/2 percent; 'risks...are moving into better balance'; 'does not expect it will be appropriate to reduce the target range until it has gained greater confidence that inflation is moving sustainably toward 2 percent' [D157].
Mar 20, 2024: HOLD at 5-1/4 to 5-1/2 percent [D158].

May 1, 2024: HOLD at 5-1/4 to 5-1/2 percent; 'lack of further progress toward the Committee's 2 percent inflation objective'; announced QT slowdown — Treasury redemption cap cut from $60B to $25B beginning in June, agency cap held at $35B [D159].
Jun 12, 2024: HOLD at 5-1/4 to 5-1/2 percent; 'modest further progress toward the Committee's 2 percent inflation objective' [D160].
Jul 31, 2024: HOLD at 5-1/4 to 5-1/2 percent; inflation 'remains somewhat elevated'; risk language shifts to 'attentive to the risks to both sides of its dual mandate' [D161].

Sep 18, 2024: CUT 50 bps to 4-3/4 to 5 percent — start of easing cycle; 'gained greater confidence that inflation is moving sustainably toward 2 percent'; 'risks...are roughly in balance'; Bowman dissented (preferred 25 bps cut) [D162].
Nov 7, 2024: CUT 25 bps to 4-1/2 to 4-3/4 percent [D163].
Dec 18, 2024: CUT 25 bps to 4-1/4 to 4-1/2 percent; Hammack dissented (preferred to hold) [D164].
Balance sheet: QT (reduction of Treasury and agency holdings) continued throughout; May 2024 statement slowed the Treasury runoff pace [D159].

Commitment language: 'strongly committed to returning inflation to its 2 percent objective' (2023–Jul 2024) changed to 'strongly committed to supporting maximum employment and returning inflation to its 2 percent objective' (from Sep 2024) [D162].

data.answer: I extracted the median projections from Table 1 of each of the 13 SEPs from March 22, 2023 through March 18, 2026 (the two most recent, June 17, 2026 and September 16, 2026, were not read before the step budget was reached). The FOMC's projected policy path evolved in three clear phases. (1) Hikes/peak: In March 2023 the median fed funds rate was 5.1% for end-2023, and it rose to 5.6% by June and September 2023 — the Committee still expected further tightening into 2024 (5.1% end-2024 in September 2023). (2) Holds: By December 2023 the 2024 median had fallen to 4.6%, and through 2024 the path showed a gradual decline (e.g., 4.6% end-2024 / 3.9% end-2025 in March 2024; 4.4% / 3.4% in September 2024), i.e., a hold at the peak followed by modest cuts. (3) Cuts: From late 2024 into 2025 the projected path shifted decisively to cuts — the 2025 median fell from 3.9% (March 2025) to 3.6% (June and September 2025, December 2025) and 3.4% (March 2026), with the longer-run rate drifting down from 2.5% (2023) to 3.0% (2024-25) and 3.1% (March 2026). The macro outlook tracked this: GDP growth was revised down in 2023 (0.4% median) then up (2.1-2.6% in late 2023-early 2024), inflation (PCE) peaked at 3.3% (2023) and core PCE at 3.9% (June 2023), then declined steadily toward 2.0-2.7% by 2026, while unemployment was projected to stay near 4.0-4.5% throughout.
data.gaps: The two most recent SEPs — June 17, 2026 (fed_sep_2026-06-17) and September 16, 2026 (fed_sep_2026-09-16) — were not read before the step budget was reached, so their median projections are not included. All 13 SEPs from March 2023 through March 2026 were fully extracted from Table 1.

data.text: I now have the opening remarks for all 10 required press conferences, plus the dot-plot figures. Let me compile the findings.

data.answer:
Across the 2023–2026 policy-turning meetings, the Chair's (Powell, then Warsh) stated rationale and forward guidance moved through four distinct phases. (1) TIGHTENING (Feb 1, 2023; Jul 26, 2023): the decision was to keep hiking (25 bps each, to 4.50–4.75% then 5.25–5.50%), justified by inflation still "well above" goal (total PCE 5.0% in Dec 2022; 3.8% in May 2023) and a labor market still "out of balance"/"very tight." Forward guidance was hawkish: "ongoing increases will be appropriate," "restoring price stability will likely require maintaining a restrictive stance for some time," and reducing inflation "is likely to require a period of below-trend growth and some softening of labor market conditions." (2) PEAK/PAUSE (Sep 20, 2023; Nov 1, 2023; Dec 13, 2023): the decision shifted to holding at 5.25–5.50% and "proceeding carefully," with the new framing that the stance was already "restrictive" and the question was "whether we need to do more." Inflation was "moderating" (PCE 3.4%) but "a long way to go"; the labor market was "rebalancing." Guidance: "prepared to tighten policy further if appropriate" (Dec), with the dot plot showing no further hikes but keeping the option on the table (median 4.6% end-2024, 3.6% end-2025, 2.9% end-2026). (3) PIVOT TO EASING (Mar 20, 2024; Sep 18, 2024; Dec 18, 2024): March was the first explicit forward guidance of a cut — "our policy rate is likely at its peak… it will likely be appropriate to begin dialing back policy restraint at some point this year," with risks "moving into better balance." September delivered the first cut (50 bps to 4.75–5.00%), framed as a "recalibration" because "upside risks to inflation have diminished, and the downside risks to employment have increased" and risks were now "roughly in balance"; the labor market was "not a source of elevated inflationary pressures." December added a 25 bps cut (to 4.25–4.50%), a full point off the peak, with the stance now "significantly less restrictive" so the Fed "can therefore be more cautious." (4) NEUTRALIZATION AND RE-ACCELERATION (Sep 17, 2025; Sep 16, 2026): September 2025 cut 25 bps to 4.00–4.25% on a "shift in the balance of risks" — "downside risks to employment have risen" (job gains 29k/mo) while "risks to inflation are tilted to the upside" from tariffs; the framework "calls for us to balance both sides." By September 16, 2026, under new Chair Warsh, the rationale had flipped back to tightening: the FOMC raised rates 25 bps to 3.75–4.00% because "inflation remains elevated" (total PCE ~3.6% in Aug 2026, "too high and has been for too long"), the labor market was "in good shape" (unemployment ~4.1%), and financial conditions were not restrictive; the Committee voted unanimously and stated it "will deliver price stability."

The overall evolution: from a one-sided, inflation-dominant, forward-leaning hawkish stance (2023) → a cautious "peak is here, we may need to do more" pause (late 2023) → a balanced, data-dependent pivot to easing with explicit "peak rate" guidance (2024) → a two-sided "balance of risks" easing toward neutral (2025) → a renewed, price-stability-first tightening under a new Chair (2026). The constant through-line was the "meeting by meeting," "not on any preset course," "totality of the data / evolving outlook / balance of risks" language, with the "balance of risks" tilting from inflation (2023) to employment (late 2024–2025) and back to inflation (2026).

Jul 26, 2023: raised 25 bps to 5.25–5.50% (peak); 'data-dependent approach in determining the extent of additional policy firming'; total PCE 3.8% (May 2023), CPI 3.0%; labor market 'very tight,' unemployment 3.6% [D104][D105][D106].

*   **March 2025:** The Treasury redemption cap was further reduced from $25 billion to $5 billion beginning in April 2025 [D137].
*   **October 2025:** The Committee decided to conclude the reduction of its aggregate securities holdings on December 1, 2025 [D142].
*   **December 2025:** The Committee initiated purchases

question: What does the Federal Reserve say about artificial intelligence?
answer:
Taking "the Federal Reserve" to mean the Board of Governors and the FOMC, and "say" to mean official publications and statements in the local 2022–2026 collection: the Fed has not mentioned AI in any formal FOMC policy statement, but it has discussed AI extensively in FOMC meeting minutes (from May 2024 through July 2026), in speeches by Governors Barr and Cook, in FEDS Notes, and in Board press releases. The core message across these sources is that AI is a general-purpose technology likely to boost productivity and potential output over time, but with considerable uncertainty about timing and magnitude, and with notable financial-stability risks tied to the concentrated, debt-financed buildout of AI infrastructure.

## FOMC deliberations (minutes)
AI first appears in the minutes in 2024 as a possible driver of productivity and disinflation, and becomes a recurring theme by 2025–2026 across three areas: the economic outlook, equity-market valuations, and financial stability.

| Meeting (minutes date) | Key points on AI |
|---|---|
| May 1, 2024 | A few participants said higher productivity growth "might be sustained by the incorporation of technologies such as artificial intelligence into existing business operations" [D132]. |
| June 12, 2024 | Disinflation factors included "the possibility of a boost to productivity associated with businesses' deployment of artificial intelligence–related technology" [D133]. |
| November 7, 2024 | Participants discussed "possible implications of the expanded use of artificial intelligence in the workplace" [D131]. |
| June 18, 2025 | "A couple of participants noted that business investment in artificial intelligence could boost productivity" [D126]. |
| July 30, 2025 | S&P 500 valuations were "mostly driven by optimism about the largest technology firms' scope to benefit from the further adoption of artificial intelligence (AI)" [D35]; "the risk that the increased use of AI in the workplace may lower employment" was cited as a downside risk to employment [D98]. |
| October 29, 2025 | Large tech stocks performed strongly "on market participants' optimism about artificial intelligence (AI)" [D38]; "advances in AI boost productivity growth while demographic factors constrain labor supply" [D104]; foreign tech stocks outperformed "largely reflecting continued investor optimism regarding AI" [D127]. |
| December 10, 2025 | "Developments regarding artificial intelligence (AI) also contributed to the volatility of the stock prices of the largest technology companies" [D39]; capital expenditures "related to AI by a set of large technology companies accelerated this year and that these firms were increasingly relying on debt to finance such expenditures" [D37]. |
| January 28, 2026 | "In light of the strong pace of AI-related investment... several participants judged that ongoing gains in productivity would be supportive of economic growth" [D103][D34]; financial-stability discussion flagged "potential vulnerabilities associated with recent developments in the AI sector, including elevated equity market valuations, high concentration of market values and activities in a small number of firms, and increased debt financing," and that "the financing of the AI-related infrastructure buildout in opaque private markets warranted monitoring" [D34]; staff noted "The financing of AI investment will likely entail higher debt issuance going forward" [D97]; emerging Asian exports surged "amid robust demand from the artificial intelligence (AI) boom" [D32]. |
| April 29, 2026 | Private credit vehicles saw net outflows "amid credit quality concerns caused in part by the potential for AI to disrupt business models in some industries, notably software" [D95]. |
| June 17, 2026 | Market developments affected by "ongoing investment in artificial intelligence (AI)" [D36]; "the possibility that AI could, over time, affect employment prospects for some classes of workers" [D101]; "the strength in business investment remained concentrated in AI-related expenditures, which showed no signs of slowing" [D101]; staff outlook flagged "uncertainty about... the potential economic effects of AI investment and adoption" [D105]. |
| July 29, 2026 | "AI-related investments would likely increase the growth of productivity and of potential output in the coming years" but "considerable uncertainty remained regarding both the timing and magnitude of potential productivity gains" [D33]; downside risk that "AI developments could disappoint, leading to a significant repricing of stocks" [D33]; financial-stability focus on "vulnerabilities associated with the financing of the rapid buildout of AI-related infrastructure," with AI capex "financed by borrowing, including credit provided by nonbank investors or regional banks" [D96]; "a few participants stressed the importance of addressing cybersecurity risks associated with rapidly advancing AI-related technologies" [D96]; "AI-related developments appeared to have had a limited net effect on employment so far" and "fears about AI leading to widespread layoffs had not materialized to date" [D102]; the AI-related infrastructure sector outperformed the S&P 500 [D31]. |

Notably, the formal FOMC policy statements for June 17, 2026 and July 29, 2026 note only that "Productivity growth and capital investment are strong" without naming AI [D92][D93].

## Governor speeches
- **Governor Michael S. Barr**, "What Will Artificial Intelligence Mean for the Labor Market and the Economy?" (New York Association for Business Economics): Barr frames AI as a normal early-stage general-purpose technology, notes that GenAI has had "relatively modest penetration thus far," but expects a "profound positive impact on productivity growth in the long term," citing one study estimating AI could contribute 0.3 to 0.9 percentage points to annual total factor productivity growth over the next decade [D51]. He concludes that "the AI boom is unlikely to be a reason for lowering policy rates" and that society must be "nimble and bold to reduce the pain of short-term dislocations for workers" [D54].
- **Governor Lisa D. Cook**, "AI: A Fed Policymaker's View" (NBER Summer Institute 2025): Cook compares AI to the printing press or electric power, notes that benchmark intelligence scores for large language models "have almost doubled over the past 12 months" and that more than half a billion users engage with an internet-based LLM weekly [D53]. She argues AI "is likely to boost productivity and could help the economy achieve higher growth while reducing inflationary pressures," while also noting AI "could boost prices in the interim, as adoption of the technology might require a surge in aggregate investment" [D52]. She describes herself as "cautiously optimistic" but emphasizes "much uncertainty remains" about the exact effects and timing [D52].

## FEDS Notes and research
- **"Monitoring AI Adoption in the US Economy"** identifies three pressing questions: how AI will affect productivity and employment, how sustainable massive AI infrastructure investment is, and which sectors are most vulnerable to disruption. It notes that as of mid-2024, point estimates of work-related AI adoption rates ranged from about 5 to 40 percent across 16 surveys [D1].
- **"Educational Exposure to Generative Artificial Intelligence"** (Jean Xiao Timmerman) examines how generative AI's effect on labor markets may influence postsecondary institutions and students, noting that high-skill and white-collar occupations may be most exposed, though it is uncertain whether higher exposure means tasks will be automated or augmented [D3].
- **"The State of AI Competition in Advanced Economies"** summarizes cross-country evidence, including that labor productivity gains from AI are expected at between 0.2 and 1.3 percentage points over the next decade depending on adoption speed, and that generative AI access reorients skills toward more productive uses with greater effects for lower-skilled workers [D4].

## Board press releases (non-policy contexts)
- **September 3, 2025**: The Board's Payments Innovation Conference (October 21, 2025) featured a panel on "the intersection of artificial intelligence and payments" [D13].
- **May 13, 2026**: The "Economic Well-Being of U.S. Households in 2025" report "discusses the adoption of generative artificial intelligence (AI) at work," finding that one in four workers used generative AI at work in the prior month and 81 percent of users agreed it saves them time [D11].
- **July 9, 2026**: The Chair's "Productivity and Jobs" task force is to "Assess the economic impact of new general-purpose technologies, including artificial intelligence, to inform the Federal Reserve's policy judgments" [D12].

## What the evidence does not cover
The searches did not return any AI mentions in FOMC policy statements (the formal decision statements) for 2023–2026, and the earliest confirmed AI references in the minutes are from May 2024. The local collection's speech and working-paper searches for additional officials (e.g., Powell, Bowman, Waller) or additional working papers on AI were not completed, so the above list of speeches and FEDS Notes may not be exhaustive.

The Board has also mentioned AI in press releases, but in a non-policy context (a payments-conference agenda and a household survey report). ## Governor speeches
- **Governor Michael S. Barr**, "What Will Artificial Intelligence Mean for the Labor Market and the Economy?" (New York Association for Business Economics): Barr frames AI as a normal early-stage general-purpose technology, notes that GenAI has had "relatively modest penetration thus far," but expects a "profound positive impact on productivity growth in the long term," citing one study estimating AI could contribute 0.3 to 0.9 percentage points to annual total factor productivity growth over the next decade [D51]. He concludes that "the AI boom is unlikely to be a reason for lowering policy rates" and that society must be "nimble and bold to reduce the pain of short-term dislocations for workers" [D54].
- **Governor Lisa D. Cook**, "AI: A Fed Policymaker's View" (NBER Summer Institute 2025): Cook compares AI to the printing press or electric power, notes that benchmark intelligence scores for large language models "have almost doubled over the past 12 months" and that more than half a billion users engage with an internet-based LLM weekly [D53]. She argues AI "is likely to boost productivity and could help the economy achieve higher growth while reducing inflationary pressures," while also noting AI "could boost prices in the interim, as adoption of the technology might require a surge in aggregate investment" [D52]. She describes herself as "cautiously optimistic" but emphasizes "much uncertainty remains" about the exact effects and timing [D52].

## FEDS Notes and research
- **"Monitoring AI Adoption in the US Economy"** identifies three pressing questions: how AI will affect productivity and employment, how sustainable massive AI infrastructure investment is, and which sectors are most vulnerable to disruption. It notes that as of mid-2024, point estimates of work-related AI adoption rates ranged from about 5 to 40 percent across 16 surveys [D1].
- **"Educational Exposure to Generative Artificial Intelligence"** (Jean Xiao Timmerman) examines how generative AI's effect on labor markets may influence postsecondary institutions and students, noting that high-skill and white-collar occupations may be most exposed, though it is uncertain whether higher exposure means tasks will be automated or augmented [D3].
- **"The State of AI Competition in Advanced Economies"** summarizes cross-country evidence, including that labor productivity gains from AI are expected at between 0.2 and 1.3 percentage points over the next decade depending on adoption speed, and that generative AI access reorients skills toward more productive uses with greater effects for lower-skilled workers [D4].

- **September 3, 2025**: The Board's Payments Innovation Conference (October 21, 2025) featured a panel on "the intersection of artificial intelligence and payments" [D13].
- **May 13, 2026**: The "Economic Well-Being of U.S. Households in 2025" report "discusses the adoption of generative artificial intelligence (AI) at work," finding that one in four workers used generative AI at work in the prior month and 81 percent of users agreed it saves them time [D11].
- **July 9, 2026**: The Chair's "Productivity and Jobs" task force is to "Assess the economic impact of new general-purpose technologies, including artificial intelligence, to inform the Federal Reserve's policy judgments" [D12].

question: How healthy is the US banking system according to the Fed?
answer:
According to the Federal Reserve's most recent assessments, the U.S. banking system is **sound, resilient, and well-capitalized**, with strong profitability and healthy loan growth. The Fed explicitly states that banks are "well positioned to continue to support a growing economy" and can absorb severe economic shocks while maintaining lending. Key vulnerabilities remain in commercial real estate (CRE) refinancing risks, elevated consumer delinquencies, and fair-value losses on fixed-rate assets, but these are described as moderate or stabilizing.

### 1. Overall Condition and Capital Strength
The Fed’s June 2026 *Supervision and Regulation Report* and May 2026 *Financial Stability Report* (FSR) both characterize the system as strong:
*   **Capital Levels:** Over 99% of all banks were "well capitalized" as of Q4 2025, with aggregate Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) ratios around **13%** for both large and small banks [D1]. The FSR notes that regulatory capital levels remain "near historically high levels" [D8][D38].
*   **Profitability:** Return on average assets (ROAA) was **1.1%** and return on equity (ROE) was **11.2%** at the end of 2025 [D4]. Large banks saw ROE rise to **14%** in Q1 2026, driven by record capital markets revenues [D6].
*   **Asset Quality:** The total loan delinquency rate was **1.6%** at the end of 2025, well below the long-run historical average of approximately **3%** [D4]. Nonperforming loan and credit loss reserve ratios declined slightly in Q1 2026 at most large banks [D6].
*   **Market Confidence:** Average credit default swap (CDS) spreads for the largest banks ended 2025 near their lowest levels since 2015, and the market leverage ratio sits near its 10-year high, indicating strong market confidence [D5].

### 2. Stress Test Results (2026)
The 2026 Dodd-Frank Act Stress Test (DFAST) confirmed that large banks have sufficient capital to weather a severe recession:
*   **No Failures:** All **32** participating banks remained above their minimum CET1 capital requirements (4.5%) under the severely adverse scenario [D47].
*   **Aggregate Resilience:** The aggregate CET1 ratio fell from an actual **12.8%** (Q4 2025) to a projected minimum of **11.2%** before recovering to **12.7%** by Q1 2028, absorbing nearly **$708 billion** in hypothetical losses [D44][D47].
*   **Bank-Level Performance:** The median projected minimum CET1 ratio across the 32 banks was **10.3%** [D35]. The five lowest projected minimum CET1 ratios were:
    1.  First Citizens Bancshares: **6.7%**
    2.  Ally Financial: **7.8%**
    3.  HSBC North America Holdings: **8.1%**
    4.  Citizens Financial Group: **8.6%**
    5.  Wells Fargo & Company and M&T Bank Corporation (tied): **9.2%** each [D18].
*   **Comparison to 2025:** For the 17 banks tested in both 2025 and 2026, 10 posted lower 2026 minimum CET1 ratios (e.g., JPMorgan Chase declined from 14.2% to 12.6%), 7 improved (e.g., BMO Financial Corp. rose from 7.8% to 10.1%), and 1 (UBS Americas Holding LLC) remained unchanged at 15.3% [D36].

### 3. Key Vulnerabilities and Risks
Despite overall strength, the Fed highlights specific areas of concern:

| Vulnerability | Fed Assessment (2026) |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Commercial Real Estate (CRE)** | Prices have stabilized after declines from mid-2022 to early 2024, but "vulnerabilities due to upcoming refinancing needs remained" [D31][D50]. CRE loan delinquencies were largely stable at the end of 2025, though they remain above 10-year averages [D34][D22]. |
| **Fair Value Losses** | Banks' available-for-sale (AFS) and held-to-maturity (HTM) portfolios were below book values by a combined **$300 billion** at the end of 2025. These losses are "still sizable and sensitive to changes in long-term interest rates" [D39][D8]. |
| **Consumer Credit** | Delinquencies on credit cards and auto loans remained above levels that have prevailed over the past decade, though they ended 2025 at lower levels than the previous year [D31][D4]. |
| **Private Credit/NDFI** | Several high-profile defaults in non-depository financial institutions (NDFI) have led to supervisory concern about the private credit sector; some banks are revisiting collateral management practices [D4]. |
| **Funding Risk** | Funding risks remained moderate. Uninsured deposits as a share of assets were significantly below the peaks seen in 2022–2023, and large banks maintained sound levels of high-quality liquid assets [D49][D8]. |

### 4. Supervisory Actions and Trends
*   **MR(I)A Review:** In February 2026, the Fed initiated a comprehensive review of all outstanding Matters Requiring Attention (MR(I)As) to align them with its new Statement of Supervisory Operating Principles (SSOP). Phase one (completed March 2026) closed fully remediated matters and downgraded others [D20][D14].
*   **Rating Trends:** Most community and regional banking organizations remain in "satisfactory" condition. Composite rating upgrades exceeded downgrades in H2 2025, and the number of outstanding MR(I)As fell to levels roughly in line with pre-2023 bank failure levels [D21].
*   **IT/Cyber Risk:** IT and operational risk MR(I)As, including cyber risk, remained the largest category of outstanding MR(I)As for community and regional banks as of Q4 2025 [D21].

In summary, the Federal Reserve views the U.S. banking system as fundamentally healthy, with capital buffers that are historically high and sufficient to absorb severe stress. The primary risks are concentrated in CRE refinancing and consumer credit delinquencies, which are being monitored closely but are not currently threatening systemic stability.

data.answer: The June 2026 Supervision and Regulation Report assesses the U.S. banking system as strong from a supervisory perspective. The Introduction states that "the U.S. banking system continues to maintain strong capital and liquidity levels while maintaining strong profitability and healthy loan growth" and that banks are "well positioned to continue to support a growing economy" (p. 9). Over 99% of banks were well capitalized at year-end 2025, with aggregate CET1 ratios around 13% for both large and small banks (p. 11). Asset quality showed only slight increases in delinquencies across several loan categories, with the total delinquency rate at 1.6%—well below the long-run average of about 3% (pp. 13–14). Profitability was healthy, with ROAA of 1.1% and ROE of 11.2% at year-end 2025, and large banks' ROE rising to 14% in Q1 2026 (pp. 14, 16). Supervisory concerns centered on NDFI/private credit exposures, CRE (especially office) concentrations, and IT/cyber risk; the Fed initiated a comprehensive MR(I)A review in February 2026 to close or downgrade matters inconsistent with its new Statement of Supervisory Operating Principles (pp. 14, 25–27).
key_facts: Introduction (p. 9): 'The U.S. banking system continues to maintain strong capital and liquidity levels while maintaining strong profitability and healthy loan growth. U.S. banks are well positioned to continue to support a growing economy.' [D29]
Over 99% of all banks were well capitalized as of Q4 2025; aggregate CET1 risk-based capital ratios were about 13% for both large and small banks, roughly unchanged from a year earlier (p. 11). [D1]
Aggregate TCE ended 2025 at a high of $2.23 trillion; unrealized losses on AFS securities fell to $98 billion, less than one-third of 2022 peak levels (p. 11). [D1]

Loan balances ended 2025 5.6% higher than a year earlier; delinquency rates increased slightly in consumer, CRE, C&I, and RRE categories, bringing the total loan delinquency rate to 1.6%, below the long-run average of about 3% (pp. 13–14). [D3][D4]
ROAA was about 1.1% and ROE about 11.2% at end of 2025, similar to recent historical experience; aggregate net interest margins increased slightly (p. 14). [D4]
Large banks' aggregate ROE rose to 14% in Q1 2026 from 12% in Q4 2025, driven by record capital markets revenues; nonperforming loan and credit loss reserve ratios declined slightly (p. 16). [D6]
Aggregate CET1 for large banks was 12% at end of Q1 2026; most banks saw QoQ declines but all remained well capitalized (p. 17). [D9]
Supervisory concern: several high-profile NDFI defaults led to concern about the private credit sector; some banks are revisiting collateral management practices for NDFI exposures (p. 14). [D4]

Most CBOs and RBOs remain in satisfactory condition; composite rating upgrades exceeded downgrades in H2 2025; outstanding MR(I)As fell notably in 2025 to levels roughly in line with pre-2023-bank-failure levels (p. 27). [D21]
IT and operational risk MR(I)As (including cyber risk) were the largest category of outstanding MR(I)As for CBOs and RBOs as of Q4 2025 (1,007 for CBOs; 154 for RBOs) (p. 27). [D21]
Supervisors continue to monitor CRE concentrations, particularly office and multifamily sectors; CRE and consumer loan delinquencies remain above 10-year averages (p. 28). [D22]

As of Dec 31, 2025, most large financial institutions were deemed satisfactory across all three LFI rating components and considered 'well-managed'; the revised LFI rating system (effective Jan 16, 2026) increased the proportion considered well-managed (p. 30). [D24]

In February 2026, the Fed initiated a comprehensive two-phase review of all outstanding safety-and-soundness MR(I)As; phase one (completed March 2026) closed fully remediated matters and downgraded/closed MR(I)As not aligned with the SSOP (pp. 25–26, Box 1). [D14][D20]
Average CDS spreads for the largest banks ended 2025 near their lowest levels since 2015 but rose in March–April 2026; the market leverage ratio sits near its 10-year high (p. 15). [D5]
data.gaps: The report does not detail specific enforcement actions (e.g., consent orders or cease-and-desist orders) by name in the sections reviewed; it discusses the MR(I)A review process and rating trends but does not enumerate individual enforcement actions taken during the period.

The median projected minimum CET1 ratio across the 32 banks is 10.3% (computed as the average of the 16th and 17th sorted values, 10.3 and 10.3). The five lowest projected minimum CET1 ratios were: First Citizens Bancshares 6.7%, Ally Financial 7.8%, HSBC North America Holdings 8.1%, Citizens Financial Group 8.6%, and Wells Fargo & M&T Bank (tied) at 9.2% each. Compared with the 2025 severely adverse scenario (22 banks in the table), 17 banks appear in both years; 10 of them posted lower 2026 minimum CET1 ratios (largest declines: JPMorgan Chase 14.2%→12.6%, -1.6 pp; Wells Fargo 10.1%→9.2%, -0.9 pp; Goldman Sachs 12.3%→11.4%, -0.9 pp), while 7 improved (largest gains: BMO 7.8%→10.1%, +2.3 pp; Capital One 9.2%→11.0%, +1.8 pp; DB USA 12.7%→14.4%, +1.7 pp) and UBS Americas was unchanged at 15.3%. Five of the 2026 bottom-five banks (First Citizens, Ally, HSBC, Citizens, KeyCorp/Huntington/Fifth Third cohort) were not in the 2025 table, so no direct 2025 comparison exists for them.

data.answer: The May 2026 Financial Stability Report (data as of April 23, 2026) concludes that the U.S. banking system "remained sound and resilient" (Overview, p. 9; Section 3, p. 33). The report's overall assessment is positive: banks hold historically high regulatory capital, have strong credit quality, and face only moderate funding risks, though fair value losses on fixed-rate assets remain sizable. Key vulnerabilities highlighted include: (1) fair value losses on banks' fixed-rate securities, which "continued to decline but were still sizable and sensitive to changes in long-term interest rates" (p. 10) — the fair values of banks' AFS and HTM portfolios were below book values by a combined $300 billion at end-2025 (p. 35); (2) commercial real estate — prices "continued to stabilize" after significant declines from mid-2022 to early 2024, but "vulnerabilities due to upcoming refinancing needs remained" (p. 10; Section 1, p. 19), and CRE loan delinquencies were "largely stable at the end of 2025" with banks modifying terms and requiring additional collateral (p. 36); (3) funding risk — banks' reliance on uninsured deposits was "well below the peaks in 2022 and early 2023" and most domestic banks maintained high levels of liquid assets (pp. 9, 43). Specific metrics/trends cited: the CET1 ratio "remained at historically high levels" (p. 34); bank return on equity stayed within recent historical ranges through Q4 2025 (p. 34); bank loan delinquency rates "remained at low levels by historical standards" and declined across key categories (p. 36); lending standards eased again in Q4 2025 per SLOOS (p. 36); the tangible common equity to tangible assets ratio was stable for G-SIBs and rose for large non-G-SIBs and regional banks (p. 35); and banks' total assets were $29.153 trillion, up 5.3% year over year (Table 3.1, p. 33). The report does not cite specific nonperforming loan percentages or bank failure counts in the passages reviewed.
key_facts: Overview conclusion: 'The banking system remained sound and resilient, with historically high regulatory capital ratios. Fair value losses on fixed-rate assets improved somewhat but stayed elevated.' (p. 9) [D7]

The Fed explicitly states that banks are "well positioned to continue to support a growing economy" and can absorb severe economic shocks while maintaining lending. Key vulnerabilities remain in commercial real estate (CRE) refinancing risks, elevated consumer delinquencies, and fair-value losses on fixed-rate assets, but these are described as moderate or stabilizing.

### 1. Overall Condition and Capital Strength
The Fed’s June 2026 *Supervision and Regulation Report* and May 2026 *Financial Stability Report* (FSR) both characterize the system as strong:
*   **Capital Levels:** Over 99% of all banks were "well capitalized" as of Q4 2025, with aggregate Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) ratios around **13%** for both large and small banks [D1]. The FSR notes that regulatory capital levels remain "near historically high levels" [D8][D38].
*   **Profitability:** Return on average assets (ROAA) was **1.1%** and return on equity (ROE) was **11.2%** at the end of 2025 [D4]. Large banks saw ROE rise to **14%** in Q1 2026, driven by record capital markets revenues [D6].
*   **Asset Quality:** The total loan delinquency rate was **1.6%** at the end of 2025, well below the long-run historical average of approximately **3%** [D4]. Nonperforming loan and credit loss reserve ratios declined slightly in Q1 2026 [D6].
*   **Market Confidence:** Average credit default swap (CDS) spreads for the largest banks ended 2025 near their lowest levels since 2015, and the market leverage ratio sits near its 10-year high, indicating strong market confidence [D5].

### 2. Stress Test Results (2026)
The 2026 Dodd-Frank Act Stress Test (DFAST) confirmed that large banks have sufficient capital to weather a severe recession:
*   **No Failures:** All **32** participating banks remained above their minimum CET1 capital requirements (4.5%) under the severely adverse scenario [D47].
*   **Aggregate Resilience:** The aggregate CET1 ratio fell from an actual **12.8%** (Q4 2025) to a projected minimum of **11.2%** before recovering to **12.7%** by Q1 2028, absorbing nearly **$708 billion** in hypothetical losses [D44][D47].
*   **Bank-Level Performance:** The median projected minimum CET1 ratio across the 32 banks was **10.3%** [D35]. The five lowest projected minimum CET1 ratios were:
    1.  First Citizens Bancshares: **6.7%**
    2.  Ally Financial: **7.8%**
    3.  HSBC North America Holdings: **8.1%**
    4.  Citizens Financial Group: **8.6%**
    5.  Wells Fargo & Company and M&T Bank Corporation (tied): **9.2%** each [D18].
*   **Comparison to 2025:** For the 17 banks tested in both 2025 and 2026, 10 posted lower 2026 minimum CET1 ratios (e.g., JPMorgan Chase declined from 14.2% to 12.6%), while 7 improved (e.g., BMO Financial Corp. rose from 7.8% to 10.1%) [D36].

### 3. Key Vulnerabilities and Risks
Despite overall strength, the Fed highlights specific areas of concern:

| Vulnerability | Fed Assessment (2026) |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Commercial Real Estate (CRE)** | Prices have stabilized after declines from mid-2022 to early 2024, but "vulnerabilities due to upcoming refinancing needs remained" [D31][D50]. CRE loan delinquencies were largely stable at the end of 2025, though they remain above 10-year averages [D34][D22]. |
| **Fair Value Losses** | Banks' available-for-sale (AFS) and held-to-maturity (HTM) portfolios were below book values by a combined **$300 billion** at the end of 2025. These losses are "still sizable and sensitive to changes in long-term interest rates" [D39][D8]. |
| **Consumer Credit** | Delinquencies on credit cards and auto loans remained above levels that have prevailed over the past decade, though they ended 2025 at lower levels than the previous year [D31][D4]. |
| **Private Credit/NDFI** | Several high-profile defaults in non-depository financial institutions (NDFI) have led to supervisory concern about the private credit sector; some banks are revisiting collateral management practices [D4]. |
| **Funding Risk** | Funding risks remained moderate. Uninsured deposits as a share of assets were significantly below the peaks seen in 2022–2023, and large banks maintained sound levels of high-quality liquid assets [D49][D8]. |

### 4. Supervisory Actions and Trends
*   **MR(I)A Review:** In February 2026, the Fed initiated a comprehensive review of all outstanding Matters Requiring Attention (MR(I)As) to align them with its new Statement of Supervisory Operating Principles (SSOP). Phase one (completed March 2026) closed fully remediated matters and downgraded others [D20][D14].
*   **Rating Trends:** Most community and regional banking organizations remain in "satisfactory" condition. Composite rating upgrades exceeded downgrades in H2 2025, and the number of outstanding MR(I)As fell to levels roughly in line with pre-2023 bank failure levels [D21].
*   **IT/Cyber Risk:** IT and operational risk MR(I)As, including cyber risk, remained the largest category of outstanding MR(I)As for community and regional banks as of Q4 2025 [D21].

In summary, the Federal Reserve views the U.S. banking system as fundamentally healthy, with capital buffers that are historically high and sufficient to absorb severe stress. The primary risks are concentrated in CRE refinancing and consumer credit delinquencies, which are being monitored closely but are not currently threatening systemic stability.

question: What is the Fed doing about stablecoins?
answer:
As of October 2026, the Federal Reserve is actively implementing the GENIUS Act (enacted July 18, 2025) by establishing a prudential regulatory framework for payment stablecoin issuers under its supervision. On September 24, 2026, the Board released two notices of proposed rulemaking (NPRs) focusing on reserve backing, capital requirements, and redemption standards [W5][W6][W13]. The Fed’s stated position, articulated by Chair Kevin Warsh and Board Governors, is that stablecoins are a significant supervisory priority requiring strict guardrails to ensure stability and consumer protection, but they are not a systemic monetary policy priority warranting central bank support or bailouts [W1][W29].

### Regulatory and Supervisory Actions

The most significant recent development is the release of two GENIUS Act implementing proposals by the Federal Reserve Board on September 24, 2026 (published in the Federal Register on September 29, 2026) [W5][W6][W14].

**1. Substantive NPR (Docket R-1899): Prudential Rules for Board-Supervised Issuers**
This proposal sets comprehensive rules for "permitted payment stablecoin issuers" (PPSIs) supervised by the Board, including subsidiaries of insured state member banks [W6][W13]. Key provisions include:
*   **Reserve Backing:** Requires one-to-one reserve backing where the aggregate fair value of reserve assets must at all times equal or exceed the par value of outstanding stablecoins. Reserves must be segregated and diversified to withstand stress [W13].
*   **Capital Requirements:** Establishes a graduated operational-risk capital charge: 2.0% on the first $20 billion, 1.5% on the next $30 billion, and 1.0% on amounts above $50 billion. It also requires a charge equal to 25% of three-year average non-reserve-asset revenue. The proposal includes provisions for the mitigation of concentration risk regarding exposures such as uninsured deposit claims or undercollateralized reverse repos [W13].
*   **Redemption and Disclosure:** Mandates a two-business-day redemption standard and monthly public reports certified by the CEO and CFO and examined by a registered public accounting firm [W13].
*   **Prohibitions:** Bans paying interest or yield solely for holding the stablecoin and includes an anti-tying prohibition [W13].

**2. Applications NPR (Docket R-1900): Bank Subsidiary Approval**
This proposal creates a tailored application process for insured state member banks seeking Fed approval to establish a subsidiary that issues payment stablecoins [W6][W13][W14].

**3. Anti-Money Laundering (AML) and Customer Identification**
In July 2026, the Fed proposed treating PPSIs as financial institutions under the Bank Secrecy Act, requiring them to maintain effective customer identification programs (comments were due August 21, 2026) [W3][W10]. This was part of a joint rulemaking with FinCEN, the OCC, FDIC, and NCUA [W10].

**Timeline and Status:**
*   **Comments Due:** Approximately November 30, 2026 [W6][W13].
*   **Effective Date:** The GENIUS Act becomes effective on the earlier of January 18, 2027, or 120 days after final implementing regulations are issued [W6][W13].
*   **State Certification:** Treasury issued an immediately effective interim final rule establishing state certification procedures for PPSIs with $10 billion or less in outstanding issuance, with initial state certifications due by January 18, 2028 [W6].

### Policy Statements and Official Views

**Chair Kevin Warsh (Took Office May 2026)**
*   **Jackson Hole Keynote (August 28, 2026):** In his first major address, delivered at the Kansas City Fed symposium themed "Financial Innovation: Implications for Payments and Policy" (the first time payments/crypto was the organizing theme), Warsh framed stablecoins as a **supervisory rather than systemic priority** [W16][W18][W20].
*   **No Bailouts:** Press coverage of the speech indicates Warsh explicitly rejected the idea of Fed bailouts for crypto or stablecoins, emphasizing that the Fed's role is supervision, not support [W29].
*   **Monetary Policy Focus:** The full transcript emphasizes monetary policy principles, noting that inflation is still running above the Fed’s 2% target, and discusses AI's economic implications, without detailed stablecoin prescriptions, reinforcing the view that stablecoins are a regulatory/supervisory issue rather than a core monetary policy tool [W16][W20].

**Governor Michael S. Barr**
*   **Statement on Proposed Rules (September 24, 2026):** Barr supported the September 2026 NPRs as a step toward strong guardrails, praising the reserve asset limitations and standardized capital requirements [W1].
*   **Key Concerns:** He urged that the final rule clearly establish **universal redemption rights** to support public confidence and flagged concerns about the "significant or systemic" AML standard, calling for stronger AML enforcement [W1].
*   **Earlier Speeches (2025):** Barr has consistently warned that stablecoins are susceptible to runs similar to banks or money market funds because they lack deposit insurance and central bank liquidity access. He emphasized that "stablecoins will only be stable if they can be reliably and promptly redeemed at par in a range of conditions," including market stress [D12][D13]. He highlighted the risk of issuers "reaching for yield" in reserve assets, particularly in low-interest-rate environments, and stressed the need for tight control over permissible reserve assets [D13][D14].

**Governor Christopher J. Waller**
*   **Speech on Maturing Market:** Waller noted that stablecoins are forms of private money subject to run risk and "depegs." He advocated for a U.S. regulatory and supervisory framework that is **proportionate to the risks** they pose, allowing both banks and non-banks to issue regulated stablecoins without stifling innovation [D11].

### Research and Analysis

*   **FEDS Note (March 30, 2026):** The Fed published a FEDS Note analyzing the benefits of payment stablecoins for cross-border payments and their implications for monetary policy implementation [W15].
*   **Interagency Coordination:** The Fed is coordinating with other federal banking agencies (OCC, FDIC, NCUA) and Treasury. The OCC and FDIC issued their own parallel GENIUS Act proposed rules in March and April 2026, respectively [W6][W7].

### Summary of Fed Stance

| Aspect | Fed Position (as of Oct 2026) |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Regulatory Framework** | Implementing GENIUS Act via two NPRs (Sept 2026) focusing on 1:1 reserves, capital, and redemption [W5][W13]. |
| **Supervisory Priority** | High; stablecoins are a key supervisory focus for the Board [W29]. |
| **Systemic Risk** | Not viewed as a systemic monetary policy priority; no Fed bailouts [W29]. |
| **Key Concerns** | Run risk, reserve asset quality, consumer protection (redemption rights), and AML compliance [W1][D13]. |
| **Innovation View** | Supportive of innovation if properly regulated; emphasizes "guardrails" and "proportionate" regulation [D11][D12]. |

The evidence does not cover any FOMC minutes or Monetary Policy Report references to stablecoins in 2025-2026, nor does it detail the specific list of eligible reserve assets in the Fed's proposal beyond the general requirement for "high-quality liquid assets" [W13].

data.answer:
As of October 2026, the Federal Reserve's primary action on stablecoins is the implementation of the GENIUS Act (enacted July 18, 2025). On September 24, 2026, the Board released two notices of proposed rulemaking (NPRs) to establish the prudential regulatory framework for payment stablecoin issuers under its supervision, focusing on reserve backing, capital requirements, and redemption standards [W5][W6][W13]. The Fed's stated position, articulated by both the new Chair and Board Governors, is that stablecoins are a significant supervisory priority requiring strict guardrails to ensure stability and consumer protection, but they are not a systemic monetary policy priority warranting central bank support or bailouts [W1][W29].

### Regulatory and Supervisory Actions

The most significant recent development is the release of two GENIUS Act implementing proposals by the Federal Reserve Board on September 24, 2026 (published in the Federal Register on September 29, 2026) [W5][W6][W14].

**1. Substantive NPR (Docket R-1899): Prudential Rules for Board-Supervised Issuers**
This proposal sets comprehensive rules for "permitted payment stablecoin issuers" (PPSIs) supervised by the Board, including subsidiaries of insured state member banks [W6][W13]. Key provisions include:
*   **Reserve Backing:** Requires one-to-one reserve backing where the aggregate fair value of reserve assets must at all times equal or exceed the par value of outstanding stablecoins. Reserves must be segregated and diversified to withstand stress [W13].
*   **Capital Requirements:** Establishes a graduated operational-risk capital charge: 2.0% on the first $20 billion, 1.5% on the next $30 billion, and 1.0% on amounts above $50 billion. It also requires a charge equal to 25% of three-year average non-reserve-asset revenue and a 2% charge on uninsured deposit claims or undercollateralized reverse repos [W13].
*   **Redemption and Disclosure:** Mandates a two-business-day redemption standard and monthly public reports certified by the CEO and CFO and examined by a registered public accounting firm [W13].
*   **Prohibitions:** Bans paying interest or yield solely for holding the stablecoin and includes an anti-tying prohibition [W13].

**2. Applications NPR (Docket R-1900): Bank Subsidiary Approval**
This proposal creates a tailored application process for insured state member banks seeking Fed approval to establish a subsidiary that issues payment stablecoins [W6][W13][W14].

**3. Anti-Money Laundering (AML) and Customer Identification**
In July 2026, the Fed proposed treating PPSIs as financial institutions under the Bank Secrecy Act, requiring them to maintain effective customer identification programs (comments were due August 21, 2026) [W3][W10]. This was part of a joint rulemaking with FinCEN, the OCC, FDIC, and NCUA [W10].

**Timeline and Status:**
*   **Comments Due:** Approximately November 30, 2026 [W6][W13].
*   **Effective Date:** The GENIUS Act becomes effective on the earlier of January 18, 2027, or 120 days after final implementing regulations are issued [W6][W13].
*   **State Certification:** Treasury issued an immediately effective interim final rule establishing state certification procedures for PPSIs with $10 billion or less in outstanding issuance, with initial state certifications due by January 18, 2028 [W6].

### Policy Statements and Official Views

**Chair Kevin Warsh (Took Office May 2026)**
*   **Jackson Hole Keynote (August 28, 2026):** In his first major address, delivered at the Kansas City Fed symposium themed "Financial Innovation: Implications for Payments and Policy" (the first time payments/crypto was the organizing theme), Warsh framed stablecoins as a **supervisory rather than systemic priority** [W16][W18][W20].
*   **No Bailouts:** Press coverage of the speech indicates Warsh explicitly rejected the idea of Fed bailouts for crypto or stablecoins, emphasizing that the Fed's role is supervision, not support [W29].
*   **Monetary Policy Focus:** The full transcript emphasizes monetary policy principles (2% PCE target, "money matters") and AI's economic implications, without detailed stablecoin prescriptions, reinforcing the view that stablecoins are a regulatory/supervisory issue rather than a core monetary policy tool [W16][W20].

**Governor Michael S. Barr**
*   **Statement on Proposed Rules (September 24, 2026):** Barr supported the September 2026 NPRs as a step toward strong guardrails, praising the reserve asset limitations and standardized capital requirements [W1].
*   **Key Concerns:** He urged that the final rule clearly establish **universal redemption rights** to support public confidence and flagged concerns about the "significant or systemic" AML standard, calling for stronger AML enforcement [W1].
*   **Earlier Speeches (2025):** Barr has consistently warned that stablecoins are susceptible to runs similar to banks or money market funds because they lack deposit insurance and central bank liquidity access. He emphasized that "stablecoins will only be stable if they can be reliably and promptly redeemed at par in a range of conditions," including market stress [D12][D13]. He highlighted the risk of issuers "reaching for yield" in reserve assets, particularly in low-interest-rate environments, and stressed the need for tight control over permissible reserve assets [D13][D14].

**Governor Christopher J. Waller**
*   **Speech on Maturing Market:** Waller noted that stablecoins are forms of private money subject to run risk and "depegs." He advocated for a U.S. regulatory and supervisory framework that is **proportionate to the risks** they pose, allowing both banks and non-banks to issue regulated stablecoins without stifling innovation [D11].

### Research and Analysis

As of October 2026, the Federal Reserve is actively implementing the GENIUS Act (enacted July 18, 2025) by establishing a prudential regulatory framework for payment stablecoin issuers under its supervision. On September 24, 2026, the Board released two notices of proposed rulemaking (NPRs) focusing on reserve backing, capital requirements, and redemption standards [W5][W6][W13]. The Fed’s stated position, articulated by Chair Kevin Warsh and Board Governors, is that stablecoins are a significant supervisory priority requiring strict guardrails to ensure stability and consumer protection, but they are not a systemic monetary policy priority warranting central bank support or bailouts [W1][W29].

### Regulatory and Supervisory Actions

The most significant recent development is the release of two GENIUS Act implementing proposals by the Federal Reserve Board on September 24, 2026 (published in the Federal Register on September 29, 2026) [W5][W6][W14].

**1. Substantive NPR (Docket R-1899): Prudential Rules for Board-Supervised Issuers**
This proposal sets comprehensive rules for "permitted payment stablecoin issuers" (PPSIs) supervised by the Board, including subsidiaries of insured state member banks [W6][W13]. Key provisions include:
*   **Reserve Backing:** Requires one-to-one reserve backing where the aggregate fair value of reserve assets must at all times equal or exceed the par value of outstanding stablecoins. Reserves must be segregated and diversified to withstand stress [W13].
*   **Capital Requirements:** Establishes a graduated operational-risk capital charge: 2.0% on the first $20 billion, 1.5% on the next $30 billion, and 1.0% on amounts above $50 billion. It also requires a charge equal to 25% of three-year average non-reserve-asset revenue. The proposal includes provisions for the mitigation of concentration risk regarding exposures such as uninsured deposit claims or undercollateralized reverse repos [W13].
*   **Redemption and Disclosure:** Mandates a two-business-day redemption standard and monthly public reports certified by the CEO and CFO and examined by a registered public accounting firm [W13].
*   **Prohibitions:** Bans paying interest or yield solely for holding the stablecoin and includes an anti-tying prohibition [W13].

**2. Applications NPR (Docket R-1900): Bank Subsidiary Approval**
This proposal creates a tailored application process for insured state member banks seeking Fed approval to establish a subsidiary that issues payment stablecoins [W6][W13][W14].

**3. Anti-Money Laundering (AML) and Customer Identification**
In July 2026, the Fed proposed treating PPSIs as financial institutions under the Bank Secrecy Act, requiring them to maintain effective customer identification programs (comments were due August 21, 2026) [W3][W10]. This was part of a joint rulemaking with FinCEN, the OCC, FDIC, and NCUA [W10].

**Timeline and Status:**
*   **Comments Due:** Approximately November 30, 2026 [W6][W13].
*   **Effective Date:** The GENIUS Act becomes effective on the earlier of January 18, 2027, or 120 days after final implementing regulations are issued [W6][W13].
*   **State Certification:** Treasury issued an immediately effective interim final rule establishing state certification procedures for PPSIs with $10 billion or less in outstanding issuance, with initial state certifications due by January 18, 2028 [W6].

### Policy Statements and Official Views

**Chair Kevin Warsh (Took Office May 2026)**
*   **Jackson Hole Keynote (August 28, 2026):** In his first major address, delivered at the Kansas City Fed symposium themed "Financial Innovation: Implications for Payments and Policy" (the first time payments/crypto was the organizing theme), Warsh framed stablecoins as a **supervisory rather than systemic priority** [W16][W18][W20].
*   **No Bailouts:** Press coverage of the speech indicates Warsh explicitly rejected the idea of Fed bailouts for crypto or stablecoins, emphasizing that the Fed's role is supervision, not support [W29].
*   **Monetary Policy Focus:** The full transcript emphasizes monetary policy principles, noting that inflation is still running above the Fed’s 2% target, and discusses AI's economic implications, without detailed stablecoin prescriptions, reinforcing the view that stablecoins are a regulatory/supervisory issue rather than a core monetary policy tool [W16][W20].

**Governor Michael S. Barr**
*   **Statement on Proposed Rules (September 24, 2026):** Barr supported the September 2026 NPRs as a step toward strong guardrails, praising the reserve asset limitations and standardized capital requirements [W1].
*   **Key Concerns:** He urged that the final rule clearly establish **universal redemption rights** to support public confidence and flagged concerns about the "significant or systemic" AML standard, calling for stronger AML enforcement [W1].
*   **Earlier Speeches (2025):** Barr has consistently warned that stablecoins are susceptible to runs similar to banks or money market funds because they lack deposit insurance and central bank liquidity access. question: What do Fed and New York Fed data say about the state of household finances?
answer:
Taking "the state of household finances" to mean the latest available data on household debt and credit, wealth and financial well-being, and consumer expectations, the picture is one of record debt levels with weakening credit quality, broadly stable but slightly below-pre-pandemic financial well-being, and a mildly cautious consumer outlook. The most recent releases are the New York Fed's Quarterly Report on Household Debt and Credit for 2026:Q2 (released August 11, 2026), the Federal Reserve's "Economic Well-Being of U.S. Households in 2025" (SHED, published May 13, 2026), the New York Fed Survey of Consumer Expectations (SCE, data through August 2026), and—on wealth—the most recent Survey of Consumer Finances (SCF) summary, "Changes in U.S. Family Finances from 2019 to 2022" (Federal Reserve Bulletin, October 2023). Note that the collection does not contain a 2025 SCF; the 2022 SCF is the latest triennial wealth/income benchmark available.

## Household debt and credit (NY Fed, 2026:Q2)

Total household debt was $18.77 trillion in 2026:Q2, essentially flat quarter-over-quarter (-0.07%) after rising from $18.20 trillion in 2025:Q1 (+3.1% over six quarters) [D3]. Growth is now concentrated in consumer credit rather than mortgages:

| Component | 2026:Q2 | Change vs. 2025:Q1 |
|---|---|---|
| Mortgage debt | $13.12 trillion | +2.4% (but down 0.56% q/q from a $13.19T peak in 2026:Q1) [D3] |
| Auto loans | $1.713 trillion | +4.3% [D3] |
| Credit cards | $1.263 trillion | +6.9% (2026:Q1 figure partly a data revision) [D3] |
| Student loans | $1.651 trillion | +1.2% (edged down from 2025:Q4) [D3] |
| Home-equity revolving | $0.459 trillion | +14.1% [D3] |

Credit quality has deteriorated across all loan types over the past year. The share of all balances 90+ days delinquent rose from 2.84% in 2025:Q1 to a peak of 3.36% in 2026:Q1, easing slightly to 3.31% in 2026:Q2 [D9]. By category (90+ days delinquent, 2025:Q1 → 2026:Q2): mortgage 0.86% → 0.99% (peaking at 1.09% in 2026:Q1); auto 4.99% → 5.49% (peak 5.60%); credit cards 12.31% → 12.92% (peak 13.12%); and student loans 7.74% → 10.60%, a steady rise and the standout trend [D9]. In the overall delinquency-status mix, the share of balances 30 days late was 1.09% in 2025:Q1 and 1.05% in 2026:Q2 (roughly flat), while the severely derogatory share rose from 1.47% to 1.99% [D4].

## Wealth, income, and financial well-being

The most recent wealth benchmark is the 2022 SCF (Bulletin, October 2023), which found broad-based improvements from 2019 to 2022: real median net worth surged 37% to $192,900—the largest increase in modern SCF history—and real mean net worth rose 23% to $1,063,700 [D6][D7]. Real median family income rose 3% to $70,300 and real mean income 15% to $141,900, with gains largest at the top [D37][D10]. The share of families that saved edged down from 59% to 56% [D33]. All financial-fragility measures improved: the median leverage ratio fell to a 20-year low of 29.2%, the median payment-to-income ratio hit a record low of 13.4%, only 6.5% of debtors had payment-to-income ratios above 40% (a record low), and 1.3% declared bankruptcy in the past five years [D30][D23].

The 2025 SHED report (published May 13, 2026) shows financial well-being stable but slightly below pre-pandemic levels: 73% of adults said they were "doing okay" or "living comfortably" financially, unchanged from 2024 but down 2 points from 2019, with declines among young adults, low-income families, and Black adults [D1][D24][D5]. Savings measures were flat year-over-year but below 2021 peaks: 63% could cover a $400 emergency with cash or equivalent (down from 68% in 2021), 55% had a rainy-day fund covering three months of expenses (down from 59% in 2021), and 35% of non-retirees said their retirement plan was on track (down from 40% in 2021) [D2][D32][D38]. Twelve percent of adults could not cover the $400 expense by any means, down from 13% in 2024 [D19]. On hardship and debt: 16% did not pay all bills in full in the prior month, 28% struggled with paying bills, 8% reported family food insufficiency, and 26% skipped medical expenses for cost (down from 28% in 2024) [D21][D38]. Credit confidence fell to 61% very confident of card approval (from 65% in 2021), and 41% of student loan borrowers required to make payments had recent payment difficulties, 76% of them for affordability reasons [D22][D17].

## Consumer expectations (NY Fed SCE, August 2026)

Consumers expect inflation to keep easing: the median one-year-ahead expected inflation rate fell to 3.58% in August 2026 (from 3.67% in June), and the median three-year-ahead rate fell to 3.19% (from 3.34% in June) [D27]. On employment, the mean probability that the U.S. unemployment rate will be higher one year from now rose to 44.4% in August 2026 (from 41.7% in June), while the mean probability of finding a job if unemployed was 45.4% and the mean probability of losing a job was 13.8% [D25][D28][D35]. On income, the median expected one-year-ahead household income growth was 2.98% (25th–75th percentile: 1.06% to 5.13%), and median expected spending growth was 5.23% [D26][D34]. Looking a year ahead, 32.6% of respondents expect to be worse off (6.8% much, 25.8% somewhat) versus 25.9% better off (3.5% much, 22.3% somewhat), with 41.5% expecting to be about the same [D36]. In short, consumers expect modest income growth that trails their inflation expectations, a somewhat higher chance of unemployment, and a roughly even split between those expecting to be better off and worse off—a mildly cautious but not pessimistic outlook. Note that the SCE does not publish a composite "consumer confidence index"; the financial-situation net balance and unemployment/job-finding probabilities above are the closest published measures.

## Bottom line

Across the four data sources, U.S. households hold record debt with growth now driven by consumer credit (auto, credit cards, home-equity) while mortgage balances have begun to decline, and credit quality has weakened across all loan types over the past year, with student loan delinquency the most persistent concern [D3][D9][D4]. Wealth and income were strong in the latest SCF benchmark (2019–2022), but the 2025 SHED shows well-being stable yet slightly below pre-pandemic levels, with savings buffers and credit confidence below 2021 peaks and hardship concentrated among lower-income, young, and Black adults [D6][D7][D1][D24][D2][D22]. Consumer expectations point to easing inflation but a softening labor market and only modest income growth, leaving households mildly cautious about the year ahead [D27][D25][D26][D36].

(2) The Federal Reserve's Survey of Consumer Finances (SCF) and the 'Economic Well-Being of U.S. Households' report (2025/2026), which provide data on wealth, income, and financial well-being, accessible via the fed_research agent (for the narrative/report) and potentially data_analyst (for the SCF tables). Additionally, the New York Fed's Survey of Consumer Expectations (SCE) provides data on inflation expectations and consumer confidence, which is part of the 'state of finances' picture. I will split this into three parallel tasks: one for the NY Fed Household Debt data (data_analyst), one for the Fed's SCF/Well-Being reports (fed_research), and one for the NY Fed Consumer Expectations data (data_analyst).
assumptions: 'State of household finances' is interpreted to include household debt levels, credit conditions, wealth/income distribution, and consumer expectations/confidence.
'Current' data refers to the most recent releases in the collection: Q2 2026 for NY Fed Household Debt, 2025/2026 for Fed Well-Being/SCF, and August 2026 for NY Fed Consumer Expectations.

data.answer: Per the NY Fed Quarterly Report on Household Debt and Credit (2026:Q2, underlying data, released 2026-08-11), total household debt was $18.77 trillion in 2026:Q2, essentially flat quarter-over-quarter (-0.07%) after rising from $18.20 trillion in 2025:Q1 (+3.1% over six quarters) [D3]. Mortgage debt, the largest component, fell to $13.12 trillion in 2026:Q2 (-0.56% q/q) from a peak of $13.19 trillion in 2026:Q1, though it is still +2.4% above 2025:Q1 [D3]. Consumer credit kept growing: auto loans rose to $1.713 trillion (+4.3% over six quarters), credit cards to $1.263 trillion (+6.9% over six quarters, with a 2026:Q1 dip to $1.242T partly reflecting a data revision), student loans edged down to $1.651 trillion (-0.4% from 2025:Q4, +1.2% over six quarters), and home-equity revolving balances climbed to $0.459 trillion (+14.1% over six quarters) [D3]. Delinquency conditions have deteriorated: the share of all balances 90+ days delinquent rose from 2.84% in 2025:Q1 to a peak of 3.36% in 2026:Q1, easing slightly to 3.31% in 2026:Q2 [D9]. Mortgage delinquency (90+) jumped from 0.86% to 1.09% over that period before easing to 0.99%; auto delinquency rose from 4.99% to 5.60% then eased to 5.49%; credit card delinquency rose from 12.31% to 13.12% then eased to 12.92%; and student loan delinquency climbed steadily from 7.74% to 10.60% [D9]. In the overall delinquency-status mix, the share of balances 30+ days late rose from ~2.0% in 2025:Q1 to ~2.7% in 2026:Q2, and the severely derogatory share rose from 1.47% to 1.99% [D4]. Overall, household debt is at record levels with growth now concentrated in consumer credit (especially auto and credit cards) while mortgage balances have begun to decline, and credit quality has weakened across all loan types over the past year, with student loan delinquency the standout trend.

Mortgage debt: $13.117T in 2026:Q2, down 0.56% q/q from $13.191T peak in 2026:Q1; +2.4% vs 2025:Q1 ($12.804T) [D3]

I did not pull the narrative report text (only the underlying data tables), so no published headline commentary is cited.

data.answer: In the New York Fed Survey of Consumer Expectations (SCE) with data through August 2026, consumers expect inflation to keep easing: the median one-year-ahead expected inflation rate fell to 3.58% in August 2026 (from 3.67% in June), and the median three-year-ahead rate fell to 3.19% (from 3.34% in June) [D27]. On employment, the mean probability that the U.S. unemployment rate will be higher one year from now rose to 44.4% in August 2026 (from 41.7% in June), while the mean probability of finding a job if unemployed was 45.4% and the mean probability of losing a job was 13.8% [D25, D28, D35]. On income, the median expected one-year-ahead household income growth was 2.98% in August 2026 (25th–75th percentile: 1.06% to 5.13%), and median expected spending growth was 5.23% [D26, D34]. Regarding their financial future, 25.8% of respondents expect to be somewhat worse off and 6.8% much worse off a year from now, versus 22.3% somewhat better off and 3.5% much better off, with 41.5% expecting to be about the same [D36]. Overall, consumers expect modest income growth that trails their inflation expectations, a somewhat higher chance of unemployment, and a roughly even split between those expecting to be better off and worse off a year from now — a mildly cautious but not pessimistic outlook. Note: the SCE workbook does not contain a composite "consumer confidence index"; the closest published measures are the financial-situation net balance and the unemployment/job-finding probabilities above.

data.answer: The collection contains two main household financial well-being reports: (1) the most recent, "Economic Well-Being of U.S. Households in 2025" (SHED, published 2026-05-13, 88 pages), and (2) the latest SCF summary, "Changes in U.S. Family Finances from 2019 to 2022" (Federal Reserve Bulletin, October 2023). The 2025 SHED report finds financial well-being stable but slightly below pre-pandemic levels: 73% of adults said they were "doing okay" or "living comfortably" financially (unchanged from 2024, down 2 points from 2019), with declines among young adults, low-income families, and Black adults [D1][D24][D5]. Savings measures were flat year-over-year but below 2021 peaks: 63% could cover a $400 emergency with cash or equivalent (down from 68% in 2021), 55% had a rainy-day fund covering three months of expenses (down from 59% in 2021), and 35% of non-retirees said their retirement plan was on track (down from 40% in 2021) [D2][D32][D38]. 12% of adults could not cover the $400 expense by any means (down from 13% in 2024) [D19]. On hardship and debt: 16% did not pay all bills in full in the prior month, 28% struggled with paying bills, 8% reported family food insufficiency, and 26% skipped medical expenses for cost [D21][D38]. Credit confidence fell to 61% very confident of card approval (from 65% in 2021), and 41% of student loan borrowers required to make payments had recent payment difficulties [D22][D17]. The 2022 SCF (the most recent triennial SCF in the collection) found broad-based improvements 2019–2022: real median net worth surged 37% to $192,900 (largest increase in modern SCF history) and real mean net worth rose 23% to $1,063,700 [D6][D7]; real median family income rose 3% to $70,300 and mean income 15% to $141,900 [D37][D10]; the share of families that saved edged down from 59% to 56% [D33]; and all financial-fragility measures improved — median leverage ratio fell to a 20-year low of 29.2%, median payment-to-income ratio hit a record low of 13.4%, only 6.5% of debtors had payment-to-income ratios above 40% (record low), and 1.3% declared bankruptcy in the past five years [D30][D23].
