data.answer:
Taking "the state of household finances" to mean the latest available data on household debt and credit, wealth and financial well-being, and consumer expectations, the picture is one of record debt levels with weakening credit quality, broadly stable but slightly below-pre-pandemic financial well-being, and a mildly cautious consumer outlook. The most recent releases are the New York Fed's Quarterly Report on Household Debt and Credit for 2026:Q2 (released August 11, 2026), the Federal Reserve's "Economic Well-Being of U.S. Households in 2025" (SHED, published May 13, 2026), the New York Fed Survey of Consumer Expectations (SCE, data through August 2026), and—on wealth—the most recent Survey of Consumer Finances (SCF) summary, "Changes in U.S. Family Finances from 2019 to 2022" (Federal Reserve Bulletin, October 2023). Note that the collection does not contain a 2025 SCF; the 2022 SCF is the latest triennial wealth/income benchmark available.

## Household debt and credit (NY Fed, 2026:Q2)

Total household debt was $18.77 trillion in 2026:Q2, essentially flat quarter-over-quarter (-0.07%) after rising from $18.20 trillion in 2025:Q1 (+3.1% over six quarters) [D3]. Growth is now concentrated in consumer credit rather than mortgages:

| Component | 2026:Q2 | Change vs. 2025:Q1 |
|---|---|---|
| Mortgage debt | $13.12 trillion | +2.4% (but down 0.56% q/q from a $13.19T peak in 2026:Q1) [D3] |
| Auto loans | $1.713 trillion | +4.3% [D3] |
| Credit cards | $1.263 trillion | +6.9% (2026:Q1 figure partly a data revision) [D3] |
| Student loans | $1.651 trillion | +1.2% (edged down from 2025:Q4) [D3] |
| Home-equity revolving | $0.459 trillion | +14.1% [D3] |

Credit quality has deteriorated across all loan types over the past year. The share of all balances 90+ days delinquent rose from 2.84% in 2025:Q1 to a peak of 3.36% in 2026:Q1, easing slightly to 3.31% in 2026:Q2 [D9]. By category (90+ days delinquent, 2025:Q1 → 2026:Q2): mortgage 0.86% → 0.99% (peaking at 1.09% in 2026:Q1); auto 4.99% → 5.49% (peak 5.60%); credit cards 12.31% → 12.92% (peak 13.12%); and student loans 7.74% → 10.60%, a steady rise and the standout trend [D9]. In the overall delinquency-status mix, the share of balances 30+ days late rose from about 2.0% in 2025:Q1 to about 2.7% in 2026:Q2, and the severely derogatory share rose from 1.47% to 1.99% [D4].

## Wealth, income, and financial well-being

The most recent wealth benchmark is the 2022 SCF (Bulletin, October 2023), which found broad-based improvements from 2019 to 2022: real median net worth surged 37% to $192,900—the largest increase in modern SCF history—and real mean net worth rose 23% to $1,063,700 [D6][D7]. Real median family income rose 3% to $70,300 and real mean income 15% to $141,900, with gains largest at the top [D37][D10]. The share of families that saved edged down from 59% to 56% [D33]. All financial-fragility measures improved: the median leverage ratio fell to a 20-year low of 29.2%, the median payment-to-income ratio hit a record low of 13.4%, only 6.5% of debtors had payment-to-income ratios above 40% (a record low), and 1.3% declared bankruptcy in the past five years [D30][D23].

The 2025 SHED report (published May 13, 2026) shows financial well-being stable but slightly below pre-pandemic levels: 73% of adults said they were "doing okay" or "living comfortably" financially, unchanged from 2024 but down 2 points from 2019, with declines among young adults, low-income families, and Black adults [D1][D24][D5]. Savings measures were flat year-over-year but below 2021 peaks: 63% could cover a $400 emergency with cash or equivalent (down from 68% in 2021), 55% had a rainy-day fund covering three months of expenses (down from 59% in 2021), and 35% of non-retirees said their retirement plan was on track (down from 40% in 2021) [D2][D32][D38]. Twelve percent of adults could not cover the $400 expense by any means, down from 13% in 2024 [D19]. On hardship and debt: 16% did not pay all bills in full in the prior month, 28% struggled with paying bills, 8% reported family food insufficiency, and 26% skipped medical expenses for cost (down from 28% in 2024) [D21][D38]. Credit confidence fell to 61% very confident of card approval (from 65% in 2021), and 41% of student loan borrowers required to make payments had recent payment difficulties, 76% of them for affordability reasons [D22][D17].

## Consumer expectations (NY Fed SCE, August 2026)

Consumers expect inflation to keep easing: the median one-year-ahead expected inflation rate fell to 3.58% in August 2026 (from 3.67% in June), and the median three-year-ahead rate fell to 3.19% (from 3.34% in June) [D27]. On employment, the mean probability that the U.S. unemployment rate will be higher one year from now rose to 44.4% in August 2026 (from 41.7% in June), while the mean probability of finding a job if unemployed was 45.4% and the mean probability of losing a job was 13.8% [D25][D28][D35]. On income, the median expected one-year-ahead household income growth was 2.98% (25th–75th percentile: 1.06% to 5.13%), and median expected spending growth was 5.23% [D26][D34]. Looking a year ahead, 32.6% of respondents expect to be worse off (6.8% much, 25.8% somewhat) versus 25.9% better off (3.5% much, 22.3% somewhat), with 41.5% expecting to be about the same [D36]. In short, consumers expect modest income growth that trails their inflation expectations, a somewhat higher chance of unemployment, and a roughly even split between those expecting to be better off and worse off—a mildly cautious but not pessimistic outlook. Note that the SCE does not publish a composite "consumer confidence index"; the financial-situation net balance and unemployment/job-finding probabilities above are the closest published measures.

## Bottom line

Across the four data sources, U.S. households hold record debt with growth now driven by consumer credit (auto, credit cards, home-equity) while mortgage balances have begun to decline, and credit quality has weakened across all loan types over the past year, with student loan delinquency the most persistent concern [D3][D9][D4]. Wealth and income were strong in the latest SCF benchmark (2019–2022), but the 2025 SHED shows well-being stable yet slightly below pre-pandemic levels, with savings buffers and credit confidence below 2021 peaks and hardship concentrated among lower-income, young, and Black adults [D6][D7][D1][D24][D2][D22]. Consumer expectations point to easing inflation but a softening labor market and only modest income growth, leaving households mildly cautious about the year ahead [D27][D25][D26][D36].

The evidence in [D4] shows the share 30 days late was 1.09% in 2025:Q1 and 1.05% in 2026:Q2. The '2.0%' and '2.7%' figures appear to be misreadings or conflations with other delinquency buckets, and the trend is actually flat/slightly down, not a rise.

question: What are the main risks to financial stability according to the Fed?
answer:
Taking "the Fed's most recent publications" to mean the May 8, 2026 Financial Stability Report (data as of April 23, 2026) and the minutes of the July 28–29, 2026 FOMC meeting, the Federal Reserve's main risks to financial stability are: (1) elevated asset valuations, especially in equities and residential real estate; (2) notable financial-sector leverage, concentrated in hedge funds and life insurers; (3) funding risks in private credit, where semi-liquid vehicles faced redemption pressure in Q1 2026; (4) AI-related risks, including high valuations, debt-financed capex, and potential broad repricing; and (5) near-term shocks from a protracted Middle East/Iran conflict (oil shock, inflation, forced tightening), higher long-term rates from rising term premiums, and cyberattacks. The July 2026 FOMC minutes reaffirmed the staff's "notable" overall vulnerability assessment and added specific participant concerns about AI financing, private credit, Treasury market volatility, and bank capital resilience.

## Asset valuations
- The May 2026 Financial Stability Report characterized asset valuation pressures as "elevated": the S&P 500 forward price-to-earnings ratio stayed in the upper range of its historical distribution, and the equity premium remained well below its historical average [D20][D27].
- Corporate bond spreads remained low by historical standards, and leveraged loan spreads, while increased, stayed below median levels [D20].
- Treasury term premiums moved higher amid geopolitical-driven volatility, reaching near the top of their 15-year range [D20][D27][D38].
- Residential real estate prices remained well above their historical relationship with fundamentals (elevated price-to-rent ratios), while commercial real estate (CRE) prices stabilized but face a large volume of maturing debt and refinancing risk, particularly in the nonagency CMBS market [D20][D37][D38].
- The July 2026 FOMC minutes' staff assessment reiterated that asset valuation pressures were "elevated," noting the equity premium was at a level only lower in recent history during the dot-com bubble [D15].

## Borrowing by businesses and households
- Vulnerabilities from business and household debt were characterized as "moderate" in both publications [D20][D9][D15].
- Total business and household debt relative to GDP fell to levels not seen since the early 2000s [D20][D9].
- Debt-servicing capacity was weaker among non-investment-grade and private firms relying on floating-rate debt (leveraged loans, private credit), with median interest coverage ratios for lower-quality business borrowers at the lower end of their historical distribution [D9][D15].
- Auto and credit card delinquencies remained above past-decade levels, and FHA (and VA) mortgage delinquencies were above pre-pandemic levels, though overall mortgage delinquency rates stayed low by historical standards [D20][D9].
- Credit performance was solid in most markets, but small business loans and commercial mortgage-backed securities continued to be somewhat weak [D15].

## Financial-sector leverage
- Leverage vulnerabilities were characterized as "notable" in both publications [D20][D15].
- Hedge fund leverage remained near all-time highs, highly concentrated in the largest funds [D20][D25][D26][D15].
- Hedge funds' repo and prime brokerage borrowing rose to record levels [D15].
- Leverage at the largest life insurers stayed in the top quartile of its historical distribution, with high exposures to riskier, less liquid asset classes making some insurers susceptible to losses if business credit quality broadly deteriorated [D20][D25][D26][D15].
- The banking system remained sound and resilient with historically high regulatory capital ratios, though fair value losses on fixed-rate assets (available-for-sale and held-to-maturity portfolios) were below book values by a combined $300 billion at end-2025, still sizable [D20][D28][D15].
- Dealer leverage stayed low [D20][D15].

## Funding risks and private credit
- Funding risks were characterized as "moderate" [D20][D15].
- Private credit is the standout funding risk: certain nontraded perpetual-life business development companies (BDCs, $306 billion in gross assets) and interval funds ($119 billion in gross assets) faced sharply increased redemption requests in Q1 2026, many far above the 5% of NAV cap, which most managers invoked, after high-profile defaults and AI-driven disruption concerns, especially in the software sector—the largest sector in private credit portfolios [D20][D27][D33][D30][D32].
- Private credit totals approximately $1.4 trillion, about 10% of U.S. nonfinancial corporate debt and about one-third of below-investment-grade debt [D33].
- Most domestic banks maintained high levels of liquid assets, with reliance on uninsured deposits well below 2023 peaks [D20][D27].
- In the July 2026 FOMC minutes, a couple of participants noted that private credit activity had slowed recently and warranted close monitoring [D18].

## AI-related risks

data.answer: The May 8, 2026 Financial Stability Report (data as of April 23, 2026) organizes vulnerabilities into four categories—asset valuations, borrowing, financial-sector leverage, and funding risks—plus near-term risks. Asset valuation pressures were "elevated": the S&P 500 forward P/E stayed in the upper range of its historical distribution with the equity premium well below its historical average; corporate bond spreads remained low by historical standards; Treasury term premiums rose to near the top of their 15-year range amid geopolitical-driven volatility; residential real estate prices remained well above fundamentals (price-to-rent ratios elevated), while commercial real estate (CRE) prices stabilized but face a large volume of maturing debt and refinancing risk, particularly in the nonagency CMBS market. Borrowing vulnerabilities were "moderate": total business and household debt/GDP fell to levels not seen since the early 2000s, but debt-servicing capacity was weaker among non-investment-grade and private firms relying on floating-rate debt (leveraged loans, private credit), and auto/credit card delinquencies remained above past-decade levels, with FHA/VA mortgage delinquencies above pre-pandemic levels. Financial-sector leverage vulnerabilities were "notable": hedge fund leverage was near all-time highs and concentrated in the largest funds; the largest life insurers' leverage stayed in the top quartile of its historical distribution; banks remained sound with historically high capital, though fair value losses on fixed-rate assets (about $300 billion below book for AFS+HTM) stayed sizable. Funding risks were "moderate," with the standout being private credit: certain nontraded perpetual-life BDCs and interval funds faced sharply increased redemption requests in Q1 2026 (many far above the 5% of NAV cap, which most managers invoked) after high-profile defaults and AI-driven disruption concerns, especially in the software sector—the largest sector in private credit portfolios. Near-term risks highlighted: (1) a protracted Middle East/Iran conflict causing an oil shock, persistent inflation, and possible forced monetary tightening; (2) higher-than-expected long-term interest rates from rising term premiums; and (3) cyberattacks, which respondents flagged as having the most severe potential consequences. A NY Fed survey of 20 market contacts (March–April 2026) ranked geopolitical risks, oil shock, AI (equity valuations, debt-financed capex, labor market), private credit, and persistent inflation as the top-cited risks, with a risk-asset correction (potentially triggered by AI valuations or the Iran conflict) also widely cited.

The July 2026 FOMC minutes reaffirmed the staff's "notable" overall vulnerability assessment and added specific participant concerns about AI financing, private credit, Treasury market volatility, and bank capital resilience.

- The May 2026 Financial Stability Report characterized asset valuation pressures as "elevated": the S&P 500 forward price-to-earnings ratio stayed in the upper range of its historical distribution, and the equity premium remained well below its historical average [D20][D27].

- The July 2026 FOMC minutes' staff assessment reiterated that asset valuation pressures were "elevated," noting the equity premium was at a level only lower in recent history during the dot-com bubble [D15].

## Borrowing by businesses and households
- Vulnerabilities from business and household debt were characterized as "moderate" in both publications [D20][D9][D15].
- Total business and household debt relative to GDP fell to levels not seen since the early 2000s [D20][D9].
- Debt-servicing capacity was weaker among non-investment-grade and private firms relying on floating-rate debt (leveraged loans, private credit), with median interest coverage ratios for lower-quality business borrowers at the lower end of their historical distribution [D9][D15].

## AI-related risks
- The July 2026 FOMC minutes' financial stability discussion centered on AI-related risks: high equity valuations of AI-linked firms, the risk that major downward revisions to earnings assessments might lead to broad-based asset repricing, tighter financial conditions, and strains in financial institutions directly or indirectly exposed to the sector [D17][D18].
- A few participants highlighted increased borrowing to finance AI-sector capex, including credit from nonbank investors or regional banks [D18].
- A few participants stressed the importance of addressing cybersecurity risks associated with rapidly advancing AI-related technologies [D18].

## Near-term risks
- A protracted Middle East/Iran conflict could cause an oil shock, persistent inflation, and possible forced monetary tightening, with spillovers including a pullback from riskier assets, reduced dollar credit from non-U.S. banks, and sales of dollar debt securities by international investors [D35][D1][D4].

- Bank regulatory capital ratios remained within the high post-Basel III range, although the fair value of some bank assets stayed well below book value [D15].

The July 2026 FOMC minutes reaffirmed the staff's "notable" overall vulnerability assessment and added specific participant concerns about AI financing, private credit, Treasury market volatility, and bank capital resilience.

## Asset valuations
- The May 2026 Financial Stability Report characterized asset valuation pressures as "elevated": the S&P 500 forward price-to-earnings ratio stayed in the upper range of its historical distribution, and the equity premium remained well below its historical average [D20][D27].
- Corporate bond spreads remained low by historical standards, and leveraged loan spreads, while increased, stayed below median levels [D20].
- Treasury term premiums moved higher amid geopolitical-driven volatility, reaching near the top of their 15-year range [D20][D27][D38].

- The July 2026 FOMC minutes' staff assessment reiterated that asset valuation pressures were "elevated," noting the equity premium was at a level only lower in recent history during the dot-com bubble [D15].

## Borrowing by businesses and households
- Vulnerabilities from business and household debt were characterized as "moderate" in both publications [D20][D9][D15].
- Total business and household debt relative to GDP fell to levels not seen since the early 2000s [D20][D9].

question: How has the Fed's view of the labor market changed over 2026?
answer:
Taking "over 2026" to mean the period from January through September 2026 (the extent of the FOMC minutes and Beige Books available in the collection; the minutes of the September 16, 2026 FOMC meeting had not yet been released as of October 6, 2026), the Federal Reserve's view of the labor market shifted from cautious concern about downside risks in early 2026 to a clearly more confident assessment of a stable, balanced, and modestly strengthening market by mid- and late-summer. The arc ran: "stabilizing after gradual cooling" (January) → persistent downside-risk concerns (March–April) → "balanced" with eased concerns (June) → "stable, modestly strengthened" (July).

## FOMC minutes: the shift in tone

| Meeting | Assessment of conditions | Balance of risks | Key details |
|---|---|---|---|
| Jan 28, 2026 | "May be stabilizing after a period of gradual cooling"; unemployment steady, job gains low | Vast majority: downside risks had diminished; most still flagged downside risks | Low hiring and low layoffs; business contacts cautious on hiring (uncertainty, AI/automation); lower net immigration cited as a supply factor [D33]. Staff: unemployment 4.4% in December (unchanged from September); average monthly total payrolls turned negative in Q4 (government roll-off); average hourly earnings +3.8% over 12 months ending December [D56]. Statement: unemployment "shown some signs of stabilization"; members "no longer judged that downside risks to employment had risen" [D5]. Some cautioned that overly restrictive policy could risk further deterioration [D4]. |
| Mar 18, 2026 | "Broadly in balance"; unemployment little changed, job gains low | Vast majority: risks to the employment side "skewed to the downside" | Softening signs: slight rise in prime-age unemployment, job growth concentrated in health care and a few sectors, declining job-availability surveys; firms delaying/reducing hiring in anticipation of AI adoption; Middle East conflict risk to hiring [D6][D7]. February payrolls held down by a health-care strike and harsh winter weather [D6]. |
| Apr 29, 2026 | Stabilization; unemployment little changed, job gains low on average | Most: employment risks "tilted to the downside" | Debate over whether low job growth signaled fragility (several said no, commensurate with slow labor force growth; a few said yes); softness signs included sector concentration, declining job-availability surveys, and "the modest rate of wage growth" [D9]. |
| Jun 17, 2026 | "Balanced"; unemployment stable near longer-run estimates; payroll gains "strengthened this year" | Downside risks to maximum employment "had moderated a bit"; labor market "not currently a source of inflationary pressures" | Job openings, initial UI claims, layoffs stable; declines in job-finding rate and job-availability surveys reflected "relatively low dynamism"; earlier concerns about deterioration "had eased with recent data" [D13][D37]. Staff: average hourly earnings +3.4% over 12 months ending May, 0.5 pp lower than a year earlier [D57]. All supported holding the rate [D14]. |
| Jul 29, 2026 | "Stable," demand and supply in balance; "strengthened modestly" | Generally expected stability; a few noted lingering softness | Broadening of payroll gains beyond health care/social assistance, modest increases in job openings; AI had a "limited net effect" on employment and fears of widespread AI layoffs "had not materialized"; strong demand and notable wage increases for skilled workers in AI-buildout sectors (electricians, machinists, engineers); lingering softness in low job-finding rate and elevated long-term unemployment; a few flagged upside risks to wage growth [D1][D2]. |

The clearest inflection was between April and June: the explicit "skewed/tilted to the downside" risk language of March and April gave way in June to a "balanced" market with eased concerns, and by July the emphasis was on modest strengthening and stability [D7][D9][D13][D2].

## Beige Books: district-level corroboration

The district reports tracked the same trajectory, with a clear mid-year inflection:

- **January 2026:** Employment mostly unchanged (8 of 12 Districts reported no hiring change); hiring mostly backfill; temp-worker usage up; wages grew at a "moderate" pace contacts called "normal" [D44]. New York reported a slight employment decline with layoffs at major employers [D45]; Minneapolis (9th District) saw employment down slightly with weak labor demand [D16].
- **March 2026:** Employment generally stable (7 of 12 Districts no change); AI/automation cited for productivity rather than replacement; wages modest-to-moderate; rising health-insurance premiums pushed up total compensation [D55]. San Francisco (12th District) reported stable net employment with tech-sector layoffs concentrated in the Pacific Northwest and strong labor availability [D20].
- **April 2026:** Employment steady to slightly up; stable labor demand, low turnover, minimal layoffs, hiring mostly replacement; improved labor availability; AI-driven productivity let some firms delay or reduce hiring [D21]. Minneapolis improved to slightly higher employment with positive labor demand [D23].
- **June 2026:** Employment little-to-no change in 11 of 12 Districts; manufacturing (defense, data centers) the strongest hiring sector; a "low-hire, low-fire" environment; wages modest-to-moderate and in line with inflation [D39]. Minneapolis saw modest growth [D26]; St. Louis (8th District) reported unchanged employment with moderate wage growth [D25].
- **July 2026 (the inflection):** Employment rose on balance, with five Districts showing modest-to-solid gains versus only one in the prior report; gains in manufacturing, construction, and retail; skilled workers hard to find; wage growth modest-to-moderate [D27]. New York moved to modest employment gains with larger firms hiring for growth [D28]; Philadelphia (3rd District) saw manufacturing employment improve while nonmanufacturing full-time employment declined, and staffing contacts said the industry had "passed the bottom" [D29].
- **September 2026:** Employment up very slightly (three modest gains, four slight gains, five no change) with less dispersion among Districts; healthy demand in manufacturing/construction but falling demand in retail and hospitality; both positive and negative AI effects reported; wage growth modest-to-moderate [D40]. Minneapolis continued modest growth with increasing labor demand [D31]; St. Louis remained unchanged with moderate wage growth [D30].

## Wage growth

Wage growth was consistently described as modest-to-moderate and roughly in line with inflation throughout the year [D44][D55][D21][D39][D27][D40]. The only quantitative figures in the evidence are the staff-review average hourly earnings: +3.8% over the 12 months ending December 2025 (slightly below the year-earlier pace) [D56] and +3.4% over the 12 months ending May 2026, 0.5 percentage points lower than a year earlier [D57]. By June and July, participants judged nominal wage growth "consistent with inflation moving toward 2 percent" [D13][D1], with a few at the July meeting flagging upside risks to wage growth going forward [D1]. Premium pressure was noted in skilled trades, health care, and construction, and in AI-buildout sectors [D2][D40].

## Recurring themes

- **"Low-hire, low-fire":** A persistent pattern of backfill/attrition replacement rather than new positions, with workers reluctant to switch jobs amid uncertainty, from January through June [D44][D39], easing into modest new hiring by July–September [D27][D40].
- **AI:** First framed (January–April) as a tool that let firms delay or reduce hiring [D33][D21], then by July–September reported with both positive and negative effects, with fears of widespread AI-driven layoffs judged not to have materialized [D1][D40].
- **Sector rotation:** Manufacturing (defense/data-center driven) and construction were the consistent bright spots, while retail, hospitality, and technology were weak [D20][D27][D40].

## Coverage note

The evidence covers FOMC minutes for the January 28, March 18, April 29, June 17, and July 29, 2026 meetings, and Beige Books dated January 14, March 4, April 15, June 3, July 15, and September 2, 2026. The minutes of the September 16, 2026 FOMC meeting are not available in the collection (not yet released as of October 6, 2026), so the FOMC's labor market view for that meeting is not covered; the September 2026 Beige Book provides the latest district-level labor market picture [D40].

data.text: I now have the complete national labor market summaries for all six 2026 Beige Books. Let me submit my findings.

data.answer:
Across the six 2026 Beige Books, the national labor market picture moved from a flat, cautious "low-hire, low-fire" environment in early 2026 to a modest broad-based improvement by mid-2026, then to a steadier, slightly positive but less dispersed picture by September. In January, employment was mostly unchanged (8 of 12 Districts reported no hiring change), hiring was mostly backfill, temp-worker usage rose, and wages grew at a "moderate" pace that contacts called "normal" [D44]. March was similar — employment generally stable (7 of 12 Districts no change), with AI/automation cited for productivity (not replacement), modest-to-moderate wage growth, and rising health-insurance costs pushing up total compensation [D55]. April showed employment steady to slightly up with stable labor demand, low turnover, minimal layoffs, and improved labor availability, though AI-driven productivity let some firms delay or reduce hiring [D21]. June returned to little-to-no change in 11 of 12 Districts, with manufacturing (defense, data centers) the strongest hiring sector and a "low-hire, low-fire" environment [D39]. The clearest shift came in July: employment rose on balance, with five Districts showing modest-to-solid gains (versus only one in the prior report), gains in manufacturing, construction, and retail, and modest-to-moderate wage growth [D27]. September showed employment up very slightly (three modest gains, four slight gains, five no change), with less dispersion among Districts, healthy demand in manufacturing/construction but falling demand in retail and hospitality, and modest-to-moderate wage growth [D40].

Notable changes through 2026: (1) a clear mid-year inflection — the July report explicitly flagged that employment gains broadened from one District (June) to five Districts, the strongest reading of the year [D27]; (2) a persistent "low-hire, low-fire" pattern with backfill/attrition replacement rather than new positions, and workers reluctant to switch jobs due to uncertainty [D44][D39]; (3) wage growth consistently modest-to-moderate and roughly in line with inflation, with occasional cost-of-living adjustments and premium pressure in skilled trades, health care, and construction [D39][D40]; (4) a recurring theme of AI — first (Jan–Apr) framed as a tool that let firms delay or reduce hiring, and by September reported with both positive and negative effects on labor demand [D21][D40]; (5) sector rotation — manufacturing (defense/data-center driven) and construction were the consistent bright spots, while retail, hospitality, and technology (notably Pacific Northwest tech layoffs in March) were weak [D20][D27][D40].

District-level examples: New York went from a slight employment decline with layoffs at major employers (Jan) to modest employment gains with larger firms hiring for growth (Jul) [D45][D28]. Minneapolis (9th District) improved from slightly lower employment and weak labor demand (Jan) to slightly/modestly higher employment with positive labor demand (Apr–Sep) [D16][D23][D26][D31]. San Francisco (12th District) reported stable employment with tech-sector layoffs and strong labor availability (Mar) [D20]. Philadelphia (3rd District) saw nonmanufacturing full-time employment decline while manufacturing employment improved, and staffing contacts said the industry had "passed the bottom" (Jul) [D29]. St. Louis (8th District) reported unchanged employment with moderate wage growth in both June and September, amid robust price increases [D25][D30].

data.text: I now have comprehensive coverage of all four meetings, including wage growth data. Let me compile the findings.

data.answer: Across the four H1-2026 FOMC meetings, participants' labor market assessment evolved from "stabilizing after gradual cooling" (January) through a period of persistent concern about downside risks (March–April) to a clearly more confident "stable/balanced" view (June). In January, participants saw the unemployment rate holding steady with low job gains, judged conditions "may be stabilizing after a period of gradual cooling," and noted the vast majority saw downside risks to the labor market as having diminished, though most still flagged downside risks (low-hiring vulnerability, sector concentration). By March, the tone was more cautious: the market was "broadly in balance" but the vast majority judged risks to the employment side "skewed to the downside," citing prime-age unemployment uptick, health-care-concentrated job growth, and AI-related hiring caution. In April, participants again saw stabilization with low average job gains, debated whether low job growth signaled fragility, and most judged employment risks "tilted to the downside," with "modest" wage growth cited as a softness signal. By June, the tone shifted decisively more positive: payroll gains had "strengthened this year," the market was "balanced" and "not currently a source of inflationary pressures," wage growth was "consistent with inflation moving toward 2 percent," and participants noted their earlier concerns about deterioration "had eased." Wage growth was described as modest (April) and, per staff data, decelerating (3.8% y/y in Dec 2025 to 3.4% y/y in May 2026).
key_facts: Jan 28, 2026: unemployment rate held steady on net, job gains remained low; most participants saw conditions 'may be stabilizing after a period of gradual cooling'; layoffs low but hiring also low; business contacts cautious on hiring due to uncertainty and AI/automation; lower net immigration cited as a supply factor for low job gains [D33].

Jan 28, 2026: vast majority judged labor market showing signs of stabilization and that downside risks had diminished; most still noted downside risks remained (a further fall in labor demand could push unemployment sharply higher in a low-hiring environment; concentration of job gains in less cyclically sensitive sectors) [D33].

Jan 28, 2026 staff data: unemployment 4.4% in December (unchanged from September); average monthly total payrolls turned negative in Q4 (government roll-off); average hourly earnings +3.8% over 12 months ending December, slightly below year-earlier pace [D56].

Mar 18, 2026: unemployment little changed, job gains low; most judged data (job openings, layoffs, hiring, nominal wage growth) suggested labor market 'broadly in balance,' with low job growth roughly in line with slower labor force growth; February payrolls held down by health-care strike and harsh winter weather [D6].

Mar 18, 2026: several highlighted softening signs (slight rise in prime-age unemployment, job growth concentrated in health care and a few sectors, declining job-availability surveys); majority expected unemployment little changed and low net job creation, a couple expected softening; the vast majority judged risks to the employment side 'skewed to the downside'; many cited firms delaying/reducing hiring in anticipation of AI adoption; most flagged Middle East conflict risk to hiring [D7].

Apr 29, 2026: unemployment little changed, job gains low on average; most judged data (unemployment, layoffs, hiring, labor force growth) suggested stabilization; several said low job growth not necessarily fragility (commensurate with slow labor force growth), a few saw it as fragility; softness signs included sector concentration, declining job-availability surveys, and 'the modest rate of wage growth'; most judged employment risks 'tilted to the downside' [D9].

Jun 17, 2026: unemployment relatively stable over the past year near longer-run estimates; payroll employment gains 'strengthened this year' and roughly consistent with labor force growth; job openings, initial UI claims, layoffs stable, pointing to a 'balanced labor market'; declines in job-finding rate and job-availability surveys reflected 'relatively low dynamism'; many said the labor market was 'not currently a source of inflationary pressures' and nominal wage growth 'consistent with inflation moving toward 2 percent' [D13].

Jun 17, 2026: participants generally expected labor market to remain stable; some said their earlier concerns about labor market deterioration 'had eased with recent data' and solid payroll data could signal increased momentum; some cited geopolitical/uncertainty risk of reduced hiring or layoffs and AI's possible long-run employment effects [D37].
Jun 17, 2026 staff data: average hourly earnings +3.4% over 12 months ending May, 0.5 percentage point lower than a year earlier [D57].

Jun 17, 2026 policy discussion: all participants supported holding the rate; participants generally assessed upside risks to price stability remained elevated while 'downside risks to achieving maximum employment had moderated a bit' [D14].

Tone shift: January statement said unemployment 'shown some signs of stabilization' and members 'no longer judged that downside risks to employment had risen'; March and April statements kept 'attentive to the risks to both sides of its dual mandate' with employment risks explicitly skewed/tilted to the downside; by June the emphasis had flipped to a stable, balanced market with eased concerns [D5][D7][D9][D13].
data.gaps: None material. Wage growth was discussed qualitatively in the minutes (modest in April; consistent with 2% inflation in June); the only quantitative wage figures available are the staff-review average hourly earnings (3.8% y/y Dec 2025; 3.4% y/y May 2026). No participant-level wage-growth projections were stated in these minutes.

data.answer: The collection contains FOMC minutes through the 2026-07-29 meeting, but NOT the 2026-09-16 meeting (minutes are released ~3 weeks after the meeting, so the September minutes would not have been published as of today, October 6, 2026). For the 2026-07-29 meeting, participants assessed that labor market conditions were stable, with labor demand and supply in balance, and the unemployment rate had remained relatively stable over the past year near most estimates of its longer-run level [D2]. Payroll employment gains had strengthened this year and appeared roughly consistent with recent labor force growth, with layoffs, unemployment insurance claims, and hiring remaining low and stable [D2]. Some participants noted the labor market had strengthened modestly, pointing to the broadening of payroll gains to sectors beyond health care and social assistance and modest increases in job openings [D2]. Overall nominal wage growth was moderate and consistent with inflation moving toward 2 percent, though a few mentioned upside risks to wage growth going forward [D1]. A few participants noted lingering signs of softness, including the low job-finding rate and persistently elevated long-term unemployment rate [D1]. Participants generally expected labor market conditions to remain stable in the near term, with the unemployment rate staying close to current levels [D1]. Regarding AI, a few participants assessed that AI-related developments had had a limited net effect on employment so far, with some workers displaced and others benefiting from jobs created by the AI buildout, and several observed that fears about AI leading to widespread layoffs had not materialized to date [D1]. In sectors connected to the AI buildout, there was strong demand for skilled workers (electricians, machinists, engineers), leading to notable increases in their wages [D2]. Compared to earlier in 2026, there was a notable shift in tone: at the January 2026 meeting, participants cautioned that keeping policy overly restrictive could risk further deterioration in the labor market, and at the March and April 2026 meetings, the vast majority judged risks to the employment side of the mandate were skewed to the downside, with concerns about labor market fragility and AI-related hiring delays [D4][D6][D7][D9]. By July 2026, the emphasis had shifted to modest strengthening and stability, with AI viewed as having a limited net negative effect on employment rather than a source of widespread layoffs [D1][D2].

Taking "over 2026" to mean the period from January through September 2026 (the extent of the FOMC minutes and Beige Books available in the collection; the minutes of the September 16, 2026 FOMC meeting had not yet been released as of October 6, 2026), the Federal Reserve's view of the labor market shifted from cautious concern about downside risks in early 2026 to a clearly more confident assessment of a stable, balanced, and modestly strengthening market by mid- and late-summer. February payrolls held down by a health-care strike and harsh winter weather [D6]. |

| Jun 17, 2026 | "Balanced"; unemployment stable near longer-run estimates; payroll gains "strengthened this year" | Downside risks to maximum employment "had moderated a bit"; labor market "not currently a source of inflationary pressures" | Job openings, initial UI claims, layoffs stable; declines in job-finding rate and job-availability surveys reflected "relatively low dynamism"; earlier concerns about deterioration "had eased with recent data" [D13][D37]. Staff: average hourly earnings +3.4% over 12 months ending May, 0.5 pp lower than a year earlier [D57]. All supported holding the rate [D14]. |
| Jul 29, 2026 | "Stable," demand and supply in balance; "strengthened modestly" | Generally expected stability; a few noted lingering softness | Broadening of payroll gains beyond health care/social assistance, modest increases in job openings; AI had a "limited net effect" on employment and fears of widespread AI layoffs "had not materialized"; strong demand and notable wage increases for skilled workers in AI-buildout sectors (electricians, machinists, engineers); lingering softness in low job-finding rate and elevated long-term unemployment; a few flagged upside risks to wage growth [D1][D2]. |

The clearest inflection was between April and June: the explicit "skewed/tilted to the downside" risk language of March and April gave way in June to a "balanced" market with eased concerns, and by July the emphasis was on modest strengthening and stability [D7][D9][D13][D2].

## Beige Books: district-level corroboration

The district reports tracked the same trajectory, with a clear mid-year inflection:

- **January 2026:** Employment mostly unchanged (8 of 12 Districts reported no hiring change); hiring mostly backfill; temp-worker usage up; wages grew at a "moderate" pace contacts called "normal" [D44]. New York reported a slight employment decline with layoffs at major employers [D45]; Minneapolis (9th District) saw employment down slightly with weak labor demand [D16].
- **March 2026:** Employment generally stable (7 of 12 Districts no change); AI/automation cited for productivity rather than replacement; wages modest-to-moderate; rising health-insurance premiums pushed up total compensation [D55]. San Francisco (12th District) reported stable net employment with tech-sector layoffs concentrated in the Pacific Northwest and strong labor availability [D20].
- **April 2026:** Employment steady to slightly up; stable labor demand, low turnover, minimal layoffs, hiring mostly replacement; improved labor availability; AI-driven productivity let some firms delay or reduce hiring [D21]. Minneapolis improved to slightly higher employment with positive labor demand [D23].
- **June 2026:** Employment little-to-no change in 11 of 12 Districts; manufacturing (defense, data centers) the strongest hiring sector; a "low-hire, low-fire" environment; wages modest-to-moderate and in line with inflation [D39]. Minneapolis saw modest growth [D26]; St. Louis (8th District) reported unchanged employment with moderate wage growth [D25].
- **July 2026 (the inflection):** Employment rose on balance, with five Districts showing modest-to-solid gains versus only one in the prior report; gains in manufacturing, construction, and retail; skilled workers hard to find; wage growth modest-to-moderate [D27]. New York moved to modest employment gains with larger firms hiring for growth [D28]; Philadelphia (3rd District) saw manufacturing employment improve while nonmanufacturing full-time employment declined, and staffing contacts said the industry had "passed the bottom" [D29].
- **September 2026:** Employment up very slightly (three modest gains, four slight gains, five no change) with less dispersion among Districts; healthy demand in manufacturing/construction but falling demand in retail and hospitality; both positive and negative AI effects reported; wage growth modest-to-moderate [D40]. Minneapolis continued modest growth with increasing labor demand [D31]; St. Louis remained unchanged with moderate wage growth [D30].

## Wage growth

Wage growth was consistently described as modest-to-moderate and roughly in line with inflation throughout the year [D44][D55][D21][D39][D27][D40]. The only quantitative figures in the evidence are the staff-review average hourly earnings: +3.8% over the 12 months ending December 2025 (slightly below the year-earlier pace) [D56] and +3.4% over the 12 months ending May 2026, 0.5 percentage points lower than a year earlier [D57]. By June and July, participants judged nominal wage growth "consistent with inflation moving toward 2 percent" [D13][D1], with a few at the July meeting flagging upside risks to wage growth going forward [D1]. Premium pressure was noted in skilled trades, health care, and construction, and in AI-buildout sectors [D2][D40].

## Recurring themes

- **"Low-hire, low-fire":** A persistent pattern of backfill/attrition replacement rather than new positions, with workers reluctant to switch jobs amid uncertainty, from January through June [D44][D39], easing into modest new hiring by July–September [D27][D40].
- **AI:** First framed (January–April) as a tool that let firms delay or reduce hiring [D33][D21], then by July–September reported with both positive and negative effects, with fears of widespread AI-driven layoffs judged not to have materialized [D1][D40].
- **Sector rotation:** Manufacturing (defense/data-center driven) and construction were the consistent bright spots, while retail, hospitality, and technology were weak [D20][D27][D40].

## Coverage note

The evidence covers FOMC minutes for the January 28, March 18, April 29, June 17, and July 29, 2026 meetings, and Beige Books dated January 14, March 4, April 15, June 3, July 15, and September 2, 2026. The minutes of the September 16, 2026 FOMC meeting are not available in the collection (not yet released as of October 6, 2026), so the FOMC's labor market view for that meeting is not covered; the September 2026 Beige Book provides the latest district-level labor market picture [D40].

New York moved to modest employment gains with larger firms hiring for growth [D28]; Philadelphia (3rd District) saw manufacturing employment improve while nonmanufacturing full-time employment declined, and staffing contacts said the industry had "passed the bottom" [D29].
- **September 2026:** Employment up very slightly (three modest gains, four slight gains, five no change) with less dispersion among Districts; healthy demand in manufacturing/construction but falling demand in retail and hospitality; both positive and negative AI effects reported; wage growth modest-to-moderate [D40]. Minneapolis continued modest growth with increasing labor demand [D31]; St. Louis remained unchanged with moderate wage growth [D30].

## Wage growth

Wage growth was consistently described as modest-to-moderate and roughly in line with inflation throughout the year [D44][D55][D21][D39][D27][D40]. The only quantitative figures in the evidence are the staff-review average hourly earnings: +3.8% over the 12 months ending December 2025 (slightly below the year-earlier pace) [D56] and +3.4% over the 12 months ending May 2026, 0.5 percentage points lower than a year earlier [D57]. By June and July, participants judged nominal wage growth "consistent with inflation moving toward 2 percent" [D13][D1], with a few at the July meeting flagging upside risks to wage growth going forward [D1]. Premium pressure was noted in skilled trades, health care, and construction, and in AI-buildout sectors [D2][D40].

## Recurring themes

- **"Low-hire, low-fire":** A persistent pattern of backfill/attrition replacement rather than new positions, with workers reluctant to switch jobs amid uncertainty, from January through June [D44][D39], easing into modest new hiring by July–September [D27][D40].
- **AI:** First framed (January–April) as a tool that let firms delay or reduce hiring [D33][D21], then by July–September reported with both positive and negative effects, with fears of widespread AI-driven layoffs judged not to have materialized [D1][D40].
- **Sector rotation:** Manufacturing (defense/data-center driven) and construction were the consistent bright spots, while retail, hospitality, and technology were weak [D20][D27][D40].

## Coverage note

The evidence covers FOMC minutes for the January 28, March 18, April 29, June 17, and July 29, 2026 meetings, and Beige Books dated January 14, March 4, April 15, June 3, July 15, and September 2, 2026. The minutes of the September 16, 2026 FOMC meeting are not available in the collection (not yet released as of October 6, 2026), so the FOMC's labor market view for that meeting is not covered; the September 2026 Beige Book provides the latest district-level labor market picture [D40].

judge: The answer captures the main arc of the Fed's labor-market assessment in 2026—early concern about downside risk and low job gains, then a shift toward a more balanced/stable view by mid-year. However, it misses several key facts from the reference: it does not state the September FOMC statement's assessment that job gains kept pace with the workforce and unemployment changed little; it does not mention unemployment at about 4.1 percent (Warsh, August 2026); it does not mention the SEP median 2026 unemployment projection falling from 4.4 percent in March to 4.1 percent in September; and it does not clearly state that the Fed's focus moved from labor-market risk to inflation. The main point is right, but important reference details are missing.
